Multivariate Analysis Course notes for ISQS 6350 Julian F. Ludwig October 2026 Preface These notes accompany ISQS 6350 (Multivariate Analysis) at Texas Tech University. They are visual first: most ideas come with a figure, and many figures are interactive (drag a slider, press Play, rotate a 3D plot with the mouse). The course follows one thread. We observe many variables at once and want to understand why they move together. Chapter 1 sets up the language: the sample we observe, the reduced form (the distribution of the random vector behind the sample) and the structural form (the hidden forces that produce it). Chapter 2 looks at the sample, Chapter 3 at the reduced form, and the remaining chapters present structural models: principal components analysis, multidimensional scaling, factor analysis, cluster analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation models. How to use these notes Code. R code is hidden behind Code buttons; the most important code is shown directly. A figure’s code shows the complete function that draws it. Run it yourself. Each chapter starts with links to its R scripts: a figures script and the shared helpers in _common.R. Save both in one folder, set it as the working directory, and source() the figures script. Slides. The slides used in class are linked at the start of each chapter and at the bottom of the menu on the left. Use the arrow keys to move between slides; figures with a slider or a 3D view are interactive there too. Check your understanding. Each section ends with a few multiple-choice questions; click Answers to check. The packages used in the notes: install.packages(c("tidyverse", "plotly", "patchwork", "mvtnorm", "MASS", "GGally", "ggrepel", "palmerpenguins", "lattice")) Textbook Everitt, B. S. and Hothorn, T. (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Springer. The notes use different examples; each chapter lists the relevant parts of the textbook under Further reading.

An airline flies the same route, from airport A to airport B, every day. For each flight it records two numbers: the flight time and the fuel burned, both as deviations from the route’s typical flight. fig_air_data <- function() { ggplot(flights, aes(time, fuel)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey85") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey85") + geom_point(colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = 0.55, size = 2) + geom_path(data = { e <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(cov(app_X)), 1); tibble(time = e[1, ], fuel = e[2, ]) }, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.2, 4.2), ylim = c(-4.2, 4.2)) + labs(title = "200 flights on one route", subtitle = sprintf("Correlation %.2f (ellipse: one standard deviation)", num$corr), x = "flight time (min)", y = "fuel burned (100 kg)", caption = "Both variables are deviations from a typical flight on the route.") } # draw the figure fig_air_data() The cloud is tilted (correlation 0.79): longer flights tend to burn more fuel. Why do the two variables move together? 1.1.1 Why not just run a regression? The first instinct from a regression course is to treat flight time as the explanatory variable and fuel as the outcome: regress fuel on flight time and read off the slope, “one extra minute costs so much fuel”. That treats flight time as exogenous, as if someone chose it and fuel followed. Here that is not a good story. Every flight covers the same distance from A to B, so nobody chooses the flight time. Flight time and fuel are both outcomes, driven by the same underlying causes. And why a flight takes longer matters for how much more fuel it burns: If a flight takes longer because of a headwind, the plane simply spends more minutes at normal cruise, burning the manual’s 100 kg per minute. If it takes longer because it is heavier (more passengers and cargo), it climbs a little slower, but above all it burns more fuel every minute: a typical load shock adds only 12 seconds but 130 kg of fuel. cloud_base <- function(alpha = 0.25, lims = c(-4.2, 4.2)) { e <- ellipse_xy(app_root, 1) list(axes0, geom_point(data = pts, aes(x, y), colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = alpha, size = 1.4), geom_path(data = tibble(x = e[1, ], y = e[2, ]), aes(x, y), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9), coord_equal(xlim = lims, ylim = lims), labs(x = "flight time (min)", y = "fuel (100 kg)")) } f2 <- function(v) sprintf("%.2f", v) kg <- function(v) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * v) fig_regression <- function() { b <- num$beta dirs <- tibble(lab = c(sprintf("headwind: +1 min,

It describes the cloud, but it is neither the cost of a headwind nor the cost of extra load. Instead of asking how one observed variable affects the other, ask which unobserved forces move both of them, and how strongly each force moves each variable. 1.1.2 A world without relationships Suppose each flight is hit by two independent shocks, each standard normal: a headwind shock \(\varepsilon_1\) (wind stronger than usual) and a load shock \(\varepsilon_2\) (plane heavier than usual). Winds do not depend on ticket sales, so on their own these shocks form a round cloud: knowing one says nothing about the other. Press Play: the aircraft turns each flight’s two shocks into a flight time and a fuel burn, and the round cloud becomes the tilted cloud of the 200 flights above. fig_world_forward <- function(k_grid = seq(0, 1, by = 0.04), lim = 4.2) { lab <- function(k) sprintf("%.2f", k) circ <- ellipse_xy(diag(2), 1, n = 200) pts_f <- purrr::map_dfr(k_grid, function(k) { X <- app_W %*% t(matrix_power_real(air_A, k)) tibble(id = seq_len(nrow(X)), x = X[, 1], y = X[, 2], k = lab(k)) }) ell_f <- purrr::map_dfr(k_grid, function(k) { E <- matrix_power_real(air_A, k) %*% circ tibble(x = E[1, ], y = E[2, ], k = lab(k)) }) ax <- function(title) list(range = c(-lim, lim), title = title, showgrid = TRUE, gridcolor = "#ebebeb", zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "#d9d9d9", tickfont = list(size = 13), titlefont = list(size = 15)) plot_ly() |> add_trace(data = pts_f, x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~k, ids = ~id, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 7, color = "#6f7a8c", opacity = 0.55), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE) |> add_trace(data = ell_f, x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~k, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = "black", width = 2.2), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE) |> layout(xaxis = ax("headwind shock ε<sub>1</sub> → flight time (min)"), yaxis = c(ax("load shock ε<sub>2</sub> → fuel (100 kg)"), list(scaleanchor = "x")), plot_bgcolor = "white", paper_bgcolor = "white", margin = list(l = 60, r = 20, t = 20, b = 60), showlegend = FALSE) |> animation_opts(frame = 90, transition = 0, redraw = TRUE) |> animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "k = ")) |> animation_button(label = "Play") } # draw the figure fig_world_forward() Correlated data can come from independent forces: a system combines them, and because each force feeds several variables, the round cloud becomes tilted. A one-standard-deviation load shock adds about 2 tonnes: 0.20 minutes more (slower climb) and 130 kg more fuel. With fuel in units of 100 kg, each variable is a weighted sum of the same two shocks: \[  egin{aligned} X_1 = 	ext{flight time} &= 1.20\,\varepsilon_1 + 0.20\,\varepsilon_2,\ X_2 = 	ext{fuel} &= 1.20\,\varepsilon_1 + 1.30\,\varepsilon_2. \end{aligned} \] Flight time and fuel are written with capital letters, \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), because they are random: they change from flight to flight, as do the shocks. The numbers recorded for one particular flight are written in lower case, \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Chapter 3 makes this distinction precise. The same 200 flights, seen as shocks (left) and as data (right): fig_shocks_to_data <- function() { hl <- flights |> dplyr::filter(flight %in% highlight_flights) |> mutate(lab = paste("flight", flight)) p_left <- ggplot(flights, aes(headwind, load)) + geom_point(colour = "grey75", size = 1.6) + geom_point(data = hl, shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "black", size = 3.6, stroke = 1.6) + geom_text(data = hl, aes(label = lab), nudge_y = 0.38, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") + coord_equal(xlim = c(-3.6, 3.6), ylim = c(-3.6, 3.6)) + labs(title = "Shocks", subtitle = "independent", x = "headwind shock", y = "load shock") p_right <- ggplot(flights, aes(time, fuel)) + geom_point(colour = "grey75", size = 1.6) + geom_point(data = hl, shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "black", size = 3.6, stroke = 1.6) + geom_text(data = hl, aes(label = lab), nudge_y = 0.45, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") + coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.2, 4.2), ylim = c(-4.2, 4.2)) + labs(title = "Flights", subtitle = "X = A ε", x = "flight time (min)", y = "fuel (100 kg)") p_left + p_right } # draw the figure fig_shocks_to_data() In R, a matrix is filled column by column, and %*% multiplies a matrix by a vector: A <- matrix(c(1.20, 1.20, # first column: what one unit of headwind does 0.20, 1.30), # second column: what one unit of load does nrow = 2) A ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 1.2 0.2 ## [2,] 1.2 1.3 eps <- c(1, -0.5) # one flight: headwind shock +1, load shock -0.5 A %*% eps # its flight time (min) and fuel (100 kg) ## [,1] ## [1,] 1.10 ## [2,] 0.55 1.2.3 A matrix moves space Think of \(A\) not as a table of numbers but as a movement of the whole plane: every point moves, straight lines stay straight, grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin stays put. (This view comes from 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Linear Algebra.) The movement is fixed by where the two basis vectors \(e_1=(1,0)'\) and \(e_2=(0,1)'\) land, and they land on the columns of \(A\): \[ Ae_1= egin{pmatrix}1.20\1.20\end{pmatrix}, \qquad Ae_2= egin{pmatrix}0.20\1.30\end{pmatrix}. \] Every other point follows: \(X=\varepsilon_1\,Ae_1+\varepsilon_2\,Ae_2\). In R, solve() computes the inverse: solve(A) # the inverse matrix ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.9848485 -0.1515152 ## [2,] -0.9090909 0.9090909 solve(A) %*% (A %*% eps) # moves the flight back to its shocks ## [,1] ## [1,] 1.0 ## [2,] -0.5 Check your understanding In \(X=A\varepsilon\), the second column of \(A\) tells us how the second variable responds to each shock how the second shock moves all variables at once the variance of the second variable the correlation between the two variables For the flights, a one-standard-deviation headwind shock changes fuel by 130 kg 120 kg 20 kg nothing; headwind only affects time Whitening means removing outliers from the data standardising each variable separately transforming correlated variables into uncorrelated, unit-variance shocks dropping the smallest principal component Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 c. 1.3 The same data, many stories Suppose we only had the flight records, not \(A\). Can we still turn the cloud back into round, independent shocks? Yes, and in many different ways. In the figure, the left panel shows the flights with two arrows, the columns of a candidate \(A\); the right panel shows the flights moved back by that candidate, \(\varepsilon=A^{-1}X\). The slider turns both arrows together by an angle \(\varphi\); the buttons jump to the choices of the next section. fig_rotation <- function() make_rotation_figure() # draw the figure fig_rotation() The cloud of flights never moves, both arrow tips stay on the black ellipse, and the cloud on the right is always round. Every angle fits the data perfectly, so the data alone cannot tell us which arrows are the true headwind and load. 1.3.1 What the data can tell us: \(\Sigma\) The data pin down only three numbers, collected in the covariance matrix: \[ \Sigma= egin{pmatrix}\sigma_1^2 & \sigma_{12}\ \sigma_{12} & \sigma_2^2\end{pmatrix} = egin{pmatrix}1.48 & 1.70\ 1.70 & 3.13\end{pmatrix}. \] \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are the variances of flight time and fuel, \(\sigma_{12}\) their covariance, and \(ho=\sigma_{12}/(\sigma_1\sigma_2)\) the correlation. Cluster analysis (Chapter 7): a discrete latent variable, as in Section 1.7.2. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation models (Chapter 8): restrictions from theory. 1.9 Summary Regressing one variable on another assumes it is chosen from outside. When both are outcomes of the same hidden forces, ask instead which forces move them. Independent shocks form a round cloud; a system \(A\) combines them into a tilted cloud. Undoing \(A\) (whitening) recovers the shocks. The data reveal only the reduced form \(\Sigma\). Every rotation of \(A\) gives the same \(\Sigma=AA'\), so one extra restriction picks a structural form: symmetry, an ordering (regression), the longest first column, or a known coefficient. Infer (sample → reduced form) + identify (reduced form → structural form) = estimate. A structural model explains the data and can compress them. \(X=A\varepsilon\) is one structural model. Factors and clusters change the latent structure. MDS first rebuilds coordinates from the distances we care about, then the same ideas apply. Which latent coordinates make the multivariate data easier to understand? 1.9.1 Further reading 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra, chapters 1 to 3 (vectors, linear combinations, linear transformations and matrices). 2 Looking at Multivariate Data R code for this chapter: looking_at_data_figures.R (data and figures) and _common.R (shared helpers). Save both in one folder and run source("looking_at_data_figures.R"); every figure is then one function call, as shown under the Code buttons. Slides for this chapter: looking_at_data_slides.html (opens in a new tab; use the arrow keys to move between slides). In Chapter 1, data analysis moved between three layers (Section 1.5): the sample we observe, the reduced form (the distribution of the random vector that produced it) and the structural form (the hidden forces behind it). This chapter is about the first layer, the sample: how to write it down, which kinds of variables it contains, how to look at it, and how to summarise it. Chapter 3 moves to the reduced form. We follow one question from start to finish: which of the 50 US states is the most unusual? 2.1 The data matrix Multivariate data come as a table: \(n\) observations (people, firms, states, days) measured on \(p\) variables. We store them in an \(n	imes p\) data matrix \[ \mathbf X=  egin{pmatrix} x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1p}\ x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2p}\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\ x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{np} \end{pmatrix}. \] The entry \(x_{tj}\) is the value of variable \(j\) for observation \(t\): the first index is the row (observation), the second the column (variable). Row \(t\), everything we know about one observation, is written as the vector \(\mathbf x_t\): \[ \mathbf x_t= egin{pmatrix}x_{t1}\ x_{t2}\ \vdots\ x_{tp}\end{pmatrix}=(x_{t1},x_{t2},\dots,x_{tp})' . \] As in most multivariate texts (for example Johnson and Wichern, or Everitt and Hothorn), vectors are bold and numbers are not. The bold \(\mathbf x_t\) is a whole observation (a vector of \(p\) numbers); a plain letter with one subscript, such as \(x_j\), is one variable. So \(\mathbf x_1\) is “the first observation” and \(x_1\) “the first variable”; the entry \(x_{tj}\) has both indices, row first. The data matrix is the bold capital \(\mathbf X\), and the mean vector, introduced below, the bold \( ar{\mathbf x}\). Vectors in this course are columns. The prime \('\) means transpose: it turns a column into a row (and a row into a column), so \((x_{t1},\dots,x_{tp})'\) is just a compact way to write the column above on one line. Our running example ships with R: state.x77, indicators for the \(n=50\) US states in the 1970s. We use six variables that describe living conditions: income per capita, illiteracy (%), life expectancy (years), murders per 100,000 people, the share of adults with a high-school diploma (%), and the number of days with frost. Here are some of its rows: Income$ per capitaIlliteracy%Life exp.yearsMurderper 100kHS grad%Frostdays1 Alabama3,6242.169.015.141.3202 Alaska6,3151.569.311.366.71523 Arizona4,5301.870.57.858.1154 Arkansas3,3781.970.710.139.9655 California5,1141.171.710.362.620⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮43 Texas4,1882.270.912.247.435⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮50 Wyoming4,5660.670.36.962.9173 Texas is row 43, so its murder rate is \(x_{43,4}=12.2\). In R, the data matrix is simply a numeric matrix with one row per state and one column per variable: X <- state.x77[, c("Income", "Illiteracy", "Life Exp", "Murder", "HS Grad", "Frost")] dim(X) # n = 50 rows, p = 6 columns ## [1] 50 6 head(X, 3) # the first three rows ## Income Illiteracy Life Exp Murder HS Grad Frost ## Alabama 3624 2.1 69.05 15.1 41.3 20 ## Alaska 6315 1.5 69.31 11.3 66.7 152 ## Arizona 4530 1.8 70.55 7.8 58.1 15 X["Texas", ] # one row: the vector x_t ## Income Illiteracy Life Exp Murder HS Grad Frost ## 4188.0 2.2 70.9 12.2 47.4 35.0 With 50 rows and six columns, reading the numbers quickly becomes hard. Because the variables have different units (dollars, years, days), each value is first standardised: we subtract the variable’s average and divide by its standard deviation, \(z_{tj}=(x_{tj}- ar x_j)/s_j\). Draw two states in a scatterplot, lay a ruler from one point to the other, and read off the length: that is the Euclidean distance (the ordinary “straight-line” distance, with both axes drawn on the same scale). Here are Texas and California on illiteracy and murder: fig_euclid <- function() { a <- X6["California", c("Illiteracy", "Murder")]; b <- X6["Texas", c("Illiteracy", "Murder")] d <- sqrt(sum((a - b)^2)) two <- tibble(state = c("California", "Texas"), x = c(a[1], b[1]), y = c(a[2], b[2])) ggplot() + annotate("segment", x = a[1], xend = b[1], y = a[2], yend = a[2], linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") + annotate("segment", x = b[1], xend = b[1], y = a[2], yend = b[2], linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") + annotate("segment", x = a[1], xend = b[1], y = a[2], yend = b[2], colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1.4) + annotate("text", x = (a[1] + b[1]) / 2, y = a[2] - 0.18, label = sprintf("%.1f (illiteracy)", b[1] - a[1]), colour = "grey30", size = 4.5) + annotate("text", x = b[1] + 0.08, y = (a[2] + b[2]) / 2, label = sprintf("%.1f (murder)", b[2] - a[2]), colour = "grey30", size = 4.5, hjust = 0) + annotate("text", x = (a[1] + b[1]) / 2 - 0.12, y = (a[2] + b[2]) / 2 + 0.2, label = sprintf("ruler: %.2f", d), colour = col_a2, size = 4.8, hjust = 1, fontface = "bold") + geom_point(data = two, aes(x, y), colour = "black", size = 3.2) + geom_text(data = two, aes(x, y, label = state), nudge_y = 0.3, size = 4.5) + coord_equal(xlim = c(0.3, 3.3), ylim = c(9.6, 12.8)) + labs(x = "illiteracy (%)", y = "murders per 100,000", title = "A ruler between two points", subtitle = "Zoomed in, both axes on the same scale") } # draw the figure fig_euclid() The ruler is the long side of a right triangle. Its two short sides are the differences on each variable: 1.1 percentage points of illiteracy and 1.9 murders per 100,000. By Pythagoras’ theorem, \[ \sqrt{(2.2-1.1)^2+(12.2-10.3)^2}=2.20 . \] With three variables the ruler goes through space, and the same rule adds a third squared difference. With \(p\) variables we can no longer hold a ruler, but the formula carries on: square the difference on every variable, add them up, and take the square root. For observations \(s\) and \(t\), \[ \lVert \mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_tVert=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^p (x_{sj}-x_{tj})^2} . \] The same sum can be written with vectors. The difference of two observations is the column of differences, \(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_t=(x_{s1}-x_{t1},\dots,x_{sp}-x_{tp})'\). For two columns \(a\) and \(b\) of the same length, the product of the row \(a'\) with the column \(b\) multiplies matching entries and adds them up, \(a'b=\sum_{j=1}^p a_jb_j\) (a single number, the inner product). With \(a=b=\mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_t\) this is exactly the sum of squared differences, so \[ \lVert \mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_tVert=\sqrt{(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_t)'(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf x_t)} . \] The Euclidean distance depends on the units: murder rates vary over a wider range of numbers than illiteracy rates, so they dominate the distance. Standardising the variables (Section 2.5) or the Mahalanobis distance (Section 2.6.2) deal with this. X2 <- state.x77[, c("Illiteracy", "Murder")] dist(X2[c("Texas", "California"), ]) # Euclidean distance between two states ## Texas ## California 2.19545 Check your understanding In the data matrix \(\mathbf X\), the entry \(x_{tj}\) is the value of observation \(j\) on variable \(t\) the value of variable \(j\) for observation \(t\) the correlation between variables \(t\) and \(j\) the distance between observations \(t\) and \(j\) With \(p=6\) variables, each state is a point in 6-dimensional space a point in the plane a line with 6 points a 6 × 6 matrix Answers 1 b. 2 a. 2.2 Types of variables Not every column of a data set is a measurement on a number line. The traditional classification has four levels of measurement, also called measurement scales (as in Everitt and Hothorn, 2011, Chapter 1). The scale says which comparisons between two values are meaningful: only “same or different” (nominal), also “larger or smaller” (ordinal), also “by how much” (interval), and also “how many times as much” (ratio). We say a variable is nominal-scaled, ordinal-scaled, interval-scaled or ratio-scaled, or that it is measured on that scale. The examples use a second data set besides the states, the Palmer penguins (R package palmerpenguins): 333 adult penguins of three species (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo), observed on three islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, after dropping penguins with missing values. For each penguin it records the species, island, sex and year, the body mass, the flipper (wing) length, and two measurements of the bill (the beak): bill length, from the base of the bill to its tip, and bill depth, the height of the bill from top to bottom. Type What the values mean Example Nominal unordered categories (labels) penguin species, island; US region Ordinal ordered categories; the gaps are not comparable diamond cut (Fair < Good < … < Ideal); survey answer (strongly disagree < disagree < neutral < agree < strongly agree) Interval equal differences mean the same; zero is arbitrary. A step from 40 °F to 50 °F is the same change in temperature as a step from 80 °F to 90 °F. temperature in °F or °C; calendar year Ratio interval scale with a true zero, so ratios make sense. Zero means “none at all”, so a value twice as large means twice as much: 4 kg is twice 2 kg, but 80 °F is not “twice as hot” as 40 °F, because 0 °F is not “no temperature”. income, body mass (the weight shown on a scale, in grams), murder rate Two special cases are common in business data. A binary variable is a nominal variable with only two categories (default yes/no). Coded 0/1, its mean is the share of ones, which is why binary variables are often treated as numeric. A count (customer complaints, frost days) is ratio-scaled, since zero means none and 10 complaints are twice as many as 5, but it takes only whole numbers. fig_types <- function() { p_nom <- ggplot(peng, aes(island)) + geom_bar(fill = "#6f7a8c") + labs(title = "Nominal", subtitle = "Island: labels,
no order", x = NULL, y = "count") cut_med <- levels(ggplot2::diamonds$cut)[median(as.integer(ggplot2::diamonds$cut))] p_ord <- ggplot(ggplot2::diamonds, aes(cut, fill = cut == cut_med)) + geom_bar() + scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = col_a1, `FALSE` = "#6f7a8c"), guide = "none") + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) + labs(title = "Ordinal", subtitle = paste0("Diamond cut: ordered,
median '", cut_med, "'"), x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)) p_int <- ggplot(airquality, aes(Temp)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#6f7a8c", colour = "white") + labs(title = "Interval", subtitle = "Temperature (°F): zero
is arbitrary", x = "°F (New York, 1973)", y = NULL) p_rat <- ggplot(peng, aes(body_mass_g)) + geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#6f7a8c", colour = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(peng$body_mass_g), colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1) + labs(title = "Ratio", subtitle = "Body mass: true zero,
mean (red) and ratios", x = "grams", y = NULL) p_nom + p_ord + p_int + p_rat + plot_layout(nrow = 1) } # draw the figure fig_types() 2.2.1 Why the type matters The type decides what we can compute and how we can plot. Each column below is a summary or a way of showing a variable; each row a type of variable: fig_type_matrix <- function(base = 13) { sym <- c(y = "✓", n = "✗", `~` = "~") ggplot(type_matrix, aes(what, type)) + geom_tile(aes(fill = v), colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) + geom_text(aes(label = sym[v], colour = v), size = base / 2.2, fontface = "bold") + scale_fill_manual(values = c(y = "#e3f1e6", n = "#f6e3e1", `~` = "#fbf1dc"), guide = "none") + scale_colour_manual(values = c(y = "#1b7a3a", n = "#b03a2e", `~` = "#a8730f"), guide = "none") + scale_x_discrete(position = "top") + facet_grid(~ group, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "✓ works ~ with care (few categories or values, binning) ✗ meaningless") + theme_minimal(base_size = base) + theme(axis.text.x.top = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5), panel.grid = element_blank(), strip.placement = "outside", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = base), axis.text.y = element_text(size = base), plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey30")) } # draw the figure fig_type_matrix() Summaries. Means, variances, covariances and distances are built from differences and averages of values, so they need numbers on a scale: interval or ratio data. The “average island” of a penguin is meaningless, even if the computer stores the islands as 1, 2, 3. Ordinal variables such as survey scales are often treated as numeric anyway, a pragmatic choice that works when there are enough categories (factor analysis of questionnaires relies on it). Plots. A plot uses the same operations. Positions on an axis and point sizes compare distances and amounts, so they need numeric variables. Categories can only be counted, given different colours, or put in separate panels. 2.2.2 Categorical variables in R: factors A categorical variable can be stored as text, for example the island names "Biscoe", "Dream", "Torgersen" repeated for every penguin. R has a dedicated type for it, the factor. A factor stores the list of possible categories once (its levels) and, for each observation, only a whole-number code that points to a level: island_text <- as.character(palmerpenguins::penguins$island) # stored as text island <- factor(island_text) # converted to a factor levels(island) # the categories, stored once ## [1] "Biscoe" "Dream" "Torgersen" head(as.integer(island)) # each penguin only carries a code ## [1] 3 3 3 3 3 3 table(island) # counts per category ## island ## Biscoe Dream Torgersen ## 168 124 52 Converting text to a factor has several advantages: Smaller and faster. Whole-number codes take less memory than repeated text, and counting, grouping and sorting work on the codes, which is faster for large data sets. A fixed set of categories. Once the levels are set, a misspelled value ("Bisco") shows up as missing instead of silently becoming a new category, and a category with no observations still appears in counts and plots. Order. The order of the levels sets the order in tables and plot legends. For an ordinal variable, ordered = TRUE also makes comparisons such as < meaningful (see the code below). Models. Regression and other model functions recognise factors and create the dummy (0/1) variables for the categories automatically. cut <- factor(c("Good", "Ideal", "Fair"), levels = c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal"), ordered = TRUE) cut ## [1] Good Ideal Fair ## Levels: Fair < Good < Very Good < Premium < Ideal cut < "Premium" # ordered factors can be compared ## [1] TRUE FALSE TRUE R records how each column is stored: a factor is nominal (or ordinal, if ordered), a numeric is treated as interval or ratio. Storage is not meaning, though: year is stored as a number in the penguin data but is used here only as a label. sapply(palmerpenguins::penguins, class) ## species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm ## "factor" "factor" "numeric" "numeric" ## flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year ## "integer" "integer" "factor" "integer" Check your understanding Temperature in °F is an interval variable rather than a ratio variable because it can be negative its zero point is arbitrary, so “twice as hot” is meaningless it is measured with error it has only a few values Which variable should not go into a covariance matrix as it is? income in dollars murders per 100,000 penguin species coded 1, 2, 3 frost days Answers 1 b. 2 c. 2.3 A plot for each type The type of a variable also decides which plot works. The scatterplot, the workhorse for two numeric variables, breaks down as soon as a variable is categorical: fig_type_plots <- function() { cnt <- peng |> count(island, species) bad1 <- ggplot(peng, aes(island, species)) + geom_point(colour = "#6f7a8c", size = 3) + labs(title = "Scatterplot: two categorical", subtitle = sprintf("%d penguins, but only %d dots", nrow(peng), nrow(cnt)), x = "island", y = "species") good1 <- ggplot(cnt, aes(island, species)) + geom_tile(aes(fill = n), colour = "white") + geom_text(aes(label = n), size = 5) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "#eef4fa", high = col_a1, guide = "none") + labs(title = "Count table (heatmap)", subtitle = "Each combination shows its count", x = "island", y = "species") bad2 <- ggplot(peng, aes(species, body_mass_g)) + geom_point(colour = "#6f7a8c", size = 2, alpha = 0.6) + labs(title = "Scatterplot: categorical vs numeric", subtitle = "Points pile up on three lines", x = "species", y = "body mass (g)") good2 <- ggplot(peng, aes(species, body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey95") + geom_jitter(width = 0.15, colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2) + labs(title = "Boxplot with jittered points", subtitle = "Centre, spread and every penguin", x = "species", y = "body mass (g)") (bad1 + good1) / (bad2 + good2) } # draw the figure fig_type_plots() Two categorical variables (top). A scatterplot of island against species draws 333 penguins as only 5 dots: all penguins with the same combination sit on top of each other, and the plot hides how many there are. A count table (here drawn as a heatmap) shows exactly what matters: how many penguins fall into each combination. One categorical, one numeric (bottom). The points pile up on a few vertical lines and overlap. A boxplot shows the centre (median) and spread (box: middle half of the data) for each group, and jittered points (shifted sideways at random) show every penguin without overlap. Two numeric variables: the scatterplot is the right tool, one point per observation. 2.3.1 Many numeric variables: the scatterplot matrix With \(p\) numeric variables there are \(p(p-1)/2\) pairs. The scatterplot matrix shows all of them at once: the panel in row \(j\), column \(k\) plots variable \(j\) against variable \(k\), the diagonal shows each variable on its own, and the upper triangle reports the correlations (introduced below). fig_pairs <- function(base = 12) { ggpairs(states, columns = vars6, lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.1, colour = "#6f7a8c")), diag = list(continuous = wrap("densityDiag", colour = "#2c3e50")), upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 4, colour = "black", stars = FALSE)), columnLabels = labs6) + theme_minimal(base_size = base) + theme(panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey85"), axis.text = element_text(size = 7), panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) } # draw the figure fig_pairs() Illiteracy, murder, life expectancy and high-school graduation all move together, in the expected directions; frost goes with low illiteracy (northern states). With so many strong correlations, a question arises that the scatterplots alone cannot answer: are there really six separate sources of variation, or do a few common ones drive several variables at once? Principal components (Chapter 4) and factor analysis (Chapter 6) are built to answer it. Check your understanding Why is a scatterplot of two categorical variables hard to read? The axes have no units All observations with the same combination are drawn on top of each other Categorical variables cannot be plotted The points are too large Which plot suits one categorical and one numeric variable? a boxplot per group, possibly with jittered points a count table a 3D scatterplot a heatmap of the correlation matrix How many panels below the diagonal does a scatterplot matrix of 6 variables have? 6 12 15 36 Answers 1 b. 2 a. 3 c. 2.4 A third variable, in two dimensions A scatterplot matrix shows variables two at a time. To see three at once, the obvious idea is a 3D plot. 2.4.1 Why not just plot in 3D? Here are the penguins’ bill length, bill depth and flipper length in 3D, drawn from three angles: static_3d <- function(x, y, z, colour = NULL, azimuth = -35, elevation = 22, labs3 = c("x", "y", "z"), title = NULL, subtitle = NULL) { u <- function(v) (v - min(v)) / diff(range(v)) a <- azimuth * pi / 180; e <- elevation * pi / 180 proj <- function(x, y, z) { x <- x - 0.5; y <- y - 0.5; z <- z - 0.5 tibble(px = x * cos(a) - y * sin(a), py = z * cos(e) + (x * sin(a) + y * cos(a)) * sin(e)) } P <- proj(u(x), u(y), u(z)) |> mutate(col = if (is.null(colour)) "all" else as.character(colour)) edges <- list(c(0,0,0, 1,0,0), c(1,0,0, 1,1,0), c(1,1,0, 0,1,0), c(0,1,0, 0,0,0), c(0,0,0, 0,0,1), c(0,1,0, 0,1,1), c(0,0,1, 0,1,1), c(1,1,0, 1,1,1), c(0,1,1, 1,1,1)) E <- purrr::map_dfr(edges, function(v) { a0 <- proj(v[1], v[2], v[3]); a1 <- proj(v[4], v[5], v[6]) tibble(x = a0$px, y = a0$py, xend = a1$px, yend = a1$py) }) corners <- list(c(0, 0), c(0, 1), c(1, 1)) # vertical edges of the box top <- corners[[which.min(sapply(corners, function(cc) proj(cc[1], cc[2], 1)$px))]] ax <- dplyr::bind_rows(proj(0.5, -0.25, 0), proj(1.25, 0.5, 0), proj(top[1], top[2], 1.1)) |> mutate(lab = labs3, py = py - c(0.07, 0.07, 0)) # drop the label of an axis that points (almost) straight at the viewer shown <- c(abs(cos(a)), abs(sin(a)), 1) > 0.2 ax <- ax[shown, ] p <- ggplot() + geom_segment(data = E, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "grey65") + geom_point(data = P, aes(px, py, colour = col), alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) + geom_text(data = ax, aes(px, py, label = lab), size = 3.6, colour = "grey30") + coord_equal(clip = "off") + labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) if (is.null(colour)) p + scale_colour_manual(values = c(all = "#6f7a8c"), guide = "none") else p + scale_colour_manual(values = pal_species, name = NULL) } fig_3d_views <- function() { v <- function(az, el, t, s) static_3d(peng$bill_length_mm, peng$bill_depth_mm, peng$flipper_length_mm, azimuth = az, elevation = el, title = t, subtitle = s, labs3 = c("bill length", "bill depth", "flipper length")) v(-90, 0, "View 1", "Two groups?") + v(-20, 25, "View 2", "One blob?") + v(40, 60, "View 3", "Three groups?") } # draw the figure fig_3d_views() The same 333 penguins tell three different stories: two groups, one blob, three groups. On a page or a screen, a 3D plot is always a flat picture of a 3D cloud. Our eyes have to guess the depth, points hide behind each other, and values cannot be read off the axes. Rotating helps (drag the interactive version below), but it takes many views to understand one cloud, and a printed page shows only one. fig_3d <- function(height = NULL) { p <- plot_ly(peng, x = ~bill_length_mm, y = ~bill_depth_mm, z = ~flipper_length_mm, color = ~species, colors = pal_species, type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 3, opacity = 0.8), text = ~paste(species, island, sex, sep = ", "), hoverinfo = "text") |> layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "bill length"), yaxis = list(title = "bill depth"), zaxis = list(title = "flipper length"), camera = list(eye = list(x = 1.6, y = -1.6, z = 0.8))), legend = list(x = 0.02, y = 0.95), margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 10, b = 0)) if (!is.null(height)) p$height <- height p } # draw the figure fig_3d() Humans read two-dimensional pictures well: positions along two axes are what we judge most accurately. So the standard approach is to keep two axes for two of the variables and show the third in another way. Here is the penguin cloud from the 3D views, drawn the 2D way. Bill length and bill depth stay on the axes, and flipper length becomes a colour gradient from dark (short flippers) to bright (long flippers): fig_3d_in_2d <- function() { ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = flipper_length_mm)) + geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.85) + scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma", end = 0.92, name = "flipper
length (mm)") + labs(x = "bill length (mm)", y = "bill depth (mm)", title = "Two axes + a colour gradient", subtitle = "Three groups appear") } # draw the figure fig_3d_in_2d() One flat picture, and every value can be read off: there are three groups. Penguins with short bills, penguins with long and deep bills, and penguins with long but shallow bills and long flippers (bright colours). None of the three 3D views showed this clearly. A colour gradient works here because flipper length is numeric: lighter means more. Which encoding fits best depends on the type of the third variable (the plot columns of Section 2.2.1): Plot Third variable shown as Use when the third variable is grouped scatterplot colour hue, one per category categorical (species, region) bubble plot point size or colour gradient numeric (flipper length, population, income) conditioning (facet, trellis) plot separate panels, same axes categorical, or numeric cut into a few bins A categorical third variable therefore leaves a choice: colours in one panel, or one panel per category. The rest of this section looks at each plot in turn. 2.4.2 Categorical third variable: colour Mapping a categorical variable to colour gives a grouped scatterplot (in ggplot2, aes(colour = species)). Each category gets its own hue; hues have no order, which suits nominal variables. Colour can change the conclusion completely. Here are the bill measurements, first without and then with colour: fig_simpson <- function() { p_grey <- ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) + labs(title = "Ignoring species", subtitle = sprintf("r = %.2f: longer bills are shallower?", r_all), x = "bill length (mm)", y = "bill depth (mm)") p_col <- ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal_species) + labs(title = "Colour = species", subtitle = sprintf("Within each species r = %.2f to %.2f", min(r_within), max(r_within)), x = "bill length (mm)", y = "bill depth (mm)", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = c(0.84, 0.9), legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA)) p_grey + p_col } # draw the figure fig_simpson() Ignoring species, longer bills seem to be shallower (\(r=-0.23\)). Within every species the relation is positive. The negative overall correlation comes entirely from the differences between species: Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills. This reversal is Simpson’s paradox, and it is a first example of a hidden group variable, the kind of structure cluster analysis (Chapter 7) looks for. 2.4.3 Numeric third variable: size Colour hues cannot show how much, so a numeric third variable needs an encoding with an order and a scale. Mapping it to point size gives a bubble plot (aes(size = Population)); a colour gradient (light to dark) can add a fourth numeric variable. Here the states are placed by illiteracy and murder, sized by population and coloured by income: fig_bubble <- function() { big <- states |> slice_max(Population, n = 6) ggplot(states, aes(Illiteracy, Murder)) + geom_point(aes(size = Population, fill = Income), shape = 21, colour = "grey30", alpha = 0.8) + geom_text_repel(data = big, aes(label = state), size = 3.6, seed = 3, box.padding = 0.8, min.segment.length = 0) + scale_size_area(max_size = 16, breaks = c(1000, 5000, 20000), labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "k"), name = "population") + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#b35806", mid = "#f7f7f7", high = "#542788", midpoint = median(states$Income), name = "income ($)") + labs(x = "illiteracy (%)", y = "murders per 100,000") } # draw the figure fig_bubble() Bubble plots give a rough impression for a modest number of points. They crowd quickly, and sizes are hard to compare precisely (we judge areas, not lengths). 2.4.4 Categorical third variable: panels Instead of colouring by a categorical variable, we can split the data by it and draw one small scatterplot per group, all with the same axes. These are conditioning plots. The same idea goes by several names, depending on the software: facet plots in ggplot2, trellis plots in R’s lattice package (and in Everitt and Hothorn), and small multiples in general. Here body mass and flipper length are split by species and sex. Facet plot with one variable: facet_wrap(). One panel per species, side by side: fig_facet_wrap <- function() { ggplot(peng, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, colour = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) + facet_wrap(~ species) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal_species, guide = "none") + labs(x = "flipper length (mm)", y = "body mass (g)") + theme(panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey85")) } # draw the figure fig_facet_wrap() Facet plot with two variables: facet_grid(). Rows for sex, columns for species: fig_trellis <- function() { ggplot(peng, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, colour = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) + facet_grid(sex ~ species) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal_species, guide = "none") + labs(x = "flipper length (mm)", y = "body mass (g)") + theme(panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey85")) } # draw the figure fig_trellis() Trellis plot with lattice. The same plot in the older lattice package, where the formula body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm | species * sex reads “body mass against flipper length, given species and sex”: fig_lattice <- function() { lattice::xyplot(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm | species * sex, data = peng, type = c("p", "r"), col = "#6f7a8c", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, xlab = "flipper length (mm)", ylab = "body mass (g)") } # draw the figure fig_lattice() Within each panel, heavier penguins have longer flippers. Comparing panels, Gentoo penguins are larger and males are heavier than females. Check your understanding The main problem with a static 3D scatterplot is that it needs three numeric variables depth must be guessed and points hide each other, so different views suggest different structures R cannot draw 3D plots it shows too few points Bill length and depth are negatively correlated overall but positively correlated within each species. This is an example of an outlier Simpson’s paradox a nonlinear relation measurement error A conditioning (facet, trellis) plot colours points by a third variable draws one panel per group, with the same axes rotates the cloud in 3D maps a numeric variable to point size To add each state’s population to a scatterplot of illiteracy against murder, the best choice is a different colour hue for every state point size (a bubble plot) one panel per population value a static 3D plot Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 b. 4 b. 2.5 Summaries of the cloud Plots show the shape of the cloud; a few numbers summarise it. All of them are sample quantities, computed from the data matrix; Chapter 3 introduces the population quantities they estimate. 2.5.1 Mean and standard deviation The sample mean of variable \(j\) is its average over the \(n\) observations, and the mean vector collects the means of all \(p\) variables. It is the centre of the cloud: \[  ar x_j= rac1n\sum_{t=1}^n x_{tj},\qquad  ar{\mathbf x}= egin{pmatrix} ar x_1\ \vdots\  ar x_p\end{pmatrix}= rac1n\sum_{t=1}^n \mathbf x_t . \] The sample variance of variable \(j\) is the (almost) average squared deviation from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root: \[ s_j^2= rac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t=1}^n (x_{tj}- ar x_j)^2,\qquad s_j=\sqrt{s_j^2}=\sqrt{ rac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t=1}^n (x_{tj}- ar x_j)^2} . \] The standard deviation is in the units of the variable (murders per 100,000, dollars) and measures the typical distance of an observation from the mean: each \(|x_{tj}- ar x_j|\) is the distance of observation \(t\) from the mean on variable \(j\), and \(s_j\) is (almost) the square root of the average squared distance. For murder, \(s=3.69\): a typical state is about 4 murders per 100,000 away from the average of 7.4. Dividing by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\) is a small correction: deviations from the sample mean are slightly smaller than deviations from the unknown population mean. colMeans(X) # mean vector ## Income Illiteracy Life Exp Murder HS Grad Frost ## 4435.8000 1.1700 70.8786 7.3780 53.1080 104.4600 apply(X, 2, sd) # standard deviation of each column ## Income Illiteracy Life Exp Murder HS Grad Frost ## 614.4699392 0.6095331 1.3423936 3.6915397 8.0769978 51.9808481 2.5.2 Covariance The sample covariance of variables \(j\) and \(k\) is (almost) the average product of their deviations from the mean, \[ s_{jk}= rac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t=1}^n (x_{tj}- ar x_j)(x_{tk}- ar x_k). \] The sign of each product depends on the quadrant a point falls into relative to the mean. Points above average on both variables, or below on both, contribute positive products (blue); the other two quadrants contribute negative ones (red). Each product is the signed area of the rectangle between the point and the mean. fig_quadrants <- function() { cen <- states |> mutate(ci = Illiteracy - xb2[1], cm = Murder - xb2[2], prod = ci * cm, sign = ifelse(prod >= 0, "positive", "negative")) p_rect <- ggplot(cen) + geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0, xmax = ci, ymin = 0, ymax = cm, fill = sign), alpha = 0.12) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") + geom_point(aes(ci, cm, colour = sign), size = 2.2) + annotate("text", x = c(1.5, -0.9, -0.9, 1.5), y = c(8, 8, -6.5, -6.5), label = c("+", "-", "+", "-"), size = 9, colour = c(col_a1, col_a2, col_a1, col_a2)) + scale_fill_manual(values = c(positive = col_a1, negative = col_a2), guide = "none") + scale_colour_manual(values = c(positive = col_a1, negative = col_a2), guide = "none") + labs(title = "Centred data", subtitle = "Rectangle = product, sign by quadrant", x = "illiteracy - mean", y = "murder - mean") p_prod <- ggplot(cen, aes(reorder(abb, prod), prod, fill = sign)) + geom_col() + geom_hline(yintercept = s_im, linetype = 2) + annotate("label", x = 8, y = s_im + 0.2, label = sprintf("covariance = %.2f", s_im), size = 3.8, hjust = 0) + scale_fill_manual(values = c(positive = col_a1, negative = col_a2), guide = "none") + coord_flip() + labs(title = "The 50 products", subtitle = "Sum / (n - 1) = covariance", x = "states", y = "product") + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) p_rect + p_prod + plot_layout(widths = c(1.2, 1)) } # draw the figure fig_quadrants() Most states fall in the positive quadrants, so the covariance of illiteracy and murder is positive, \(s=1.58\). The covariance of a variable with itself is its variance, \(s_{jj}=s_j^2\). 2.5.3 The sample covariance matrix All variances and covariances together form the \(p	imes p\) sample covariance matrix, with the variances on the diagonal and the covariances off the diagonal: \[ S= egin{pmatrix} s_1^2 & s_{12} & \cdots & s_{1p}\ s_{21} & s_2^2 & \cdots & s_{2p}\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots\ s_{p1} & s_{p2} & \cdots & s_p^2\end{pmatrix} = rac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t=1}^n (\mathbf x_t- ar{\mathbf x})(\mathbf x_t- ar{\mathbf x})' . \] The right-hand side writes all entries at once. In Section 2.1.1 a row times a column, \(a'b\), gave a single number. The other order, a column times a row, gives a whole matrix: \(ab'\) is the \(p	imes p\) matrix with entry \(a_jb_k\) in row \(j\) and column \(k\) (the outer product). For \(a=b=\mathbf x_t- ar{\mathbf x}\), the entry in row \(j\), column \(k\) is \((x_{tj}- ar x_j)(x_{tk}- ar x_k)\), the product in the covariance formula above. Adding these matrices over all observations and dividing by \(n-1\) gives every \(s_{jk}\) at once. \(S\) is symmetric (\(s_{jk}=s_{kj}\)). It describes the shape of the cloud, just as \( ar{\mathbf x}\) describes its centre; the one-standard-deviation ellipse below is drawn from \(S\). cov(X[, c("Illiteracy", "Murder")]) # 2 x 2 covariance matrix ## Illiteracy Murder ## Illiteracy 0.3715306 1.581776 ## Murder 1.5817755 13.627465 round(cov(X), 1) # all six variables ## Income Illiteracy Life Exp Murder HS Grad Frost ## Income 377573.3 -163.7 280.7 -521.9 3076.8 7227.6 ## Illiteracy -163.7 0.4 -0.5 1.6 -3.2 -21.3 ## Life Exp 280.7 -0.5 1.8 -3.9 6.3 18.3 ## Murder -521.9 1.6 -3.9 13.6 -14.5 -103.4 ## HS Grad 3076.8 -3.2 6.3 -14.5 65.2 154.0 ## Frost 7227.6 -21.3 18.3 -103.4 154.0 2702.0 2.5.4 Correlation A covariance carries the units of both variables (dollars times days, for income and frost), which makes it hard to read. Dividing by the two standard deviations removes the units: \[ r_{jk}= rac{s_{jk}}{s_j\,s_k},\qquad -1\le r_{jk}\le 1 . \] This is the same as the covariance of the standardised values \(z_{tj}=(x_{tj}- ar x_j)/s_j\) (the values coloured in the heatmap of Section 2.1). All correlations form the \(p	imes p\) sample correlation matrix \(R\), with ones on the diagonal (every variable is perfectly correlated with itself). With \(D=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_p)\), the diagonal matrix of standard deviations, it is the covariance matrix with the units divided out: \[ R= egin{pmatrix} 1 & r_{12} & \cdots & r_{1p}\ r_{21} & 1 & \cdots & r_{2p}\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots\ r_{p1} & r_{p2} & \cdots & 1\end{pmatrix}=D^{-1}SD^{-1} . \] Here \(D^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/s_1,\dots,1/s_p)\): multiplying by it from the left divides row \(j\) of \(S\) by \(s_j\), and from the right divides column \(k\) by \(s_k\), so entry \(s_{jk}\) becomes \(s_{jk}/(s_js_k)=r_{jk}\). round(cor(X), 2) # correlation matrix ## HS Grad 0.62 -0.66 0.58 -0.49 1.00 0.37 ## Frost 0.23 -0.67 0.26 -0.54 0.37 1.00 round(cov2cor(cov(X)), 2) # the same, computed from S ## Income Illiteracy Life Exp Murder HS Grad Frost ## Income 1.00 -0.44 0.34 -0.23 0.62 0.23 ## Illiteracy -0.44 1.00 -0.59 0.70 -0.66 -0.67 ## Life Exp 0.34 -0.59 1.00 -0.78 0.58 0.26 ## Murder -0.23 0.70 -0.78 1.00 -0.49 -0.54 ## HS Grad 0.62 -0.66 0.58 -0.49 1.00 0.37 ## Frost 0.23 -0.67 0.26 -0.54 0.37 1.00 fig_cor_heat <- function() { Rdf <- as_tibble(cor(X6), rownames = "row") |> pivot_longer(-row, names_to = "col", values_to = "r") |> mutate(row = factor(row, levels = rev(vars6), labels = rev(labs6)), col = factor(col, levels = vars6, labels = labs6)) ggplot(Rdf, aes(col, row, fill = r)) + geom_tile(colour = "white") + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r), colour = abs(r) > 0.6), size = 4.3) + scale_fill_gradient2(low = col_a2, mid = "white", high = col_a1, limits = c(-1, 1)) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "black"), guide = "none") + coord_equal() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)) } # draw the figure fig_cor_heat() Move the slider to see what different correlations look like for standardised data. misses Correlation measures linear association only, and it can be driven by a single point. fig_cor_gallery <- function(nrow = 2) { make_cloud <- function(r) { M <- app_W %*% t(sym_root(sigma_of(1, 0\); the cloud next to it has no relationship at all except for one extreme point, which on its own creates a sizeable correlation. Always look at the scatterplot before trusting a correlation. Check your understanding A state that is above average on both illiteracy and murder contributes to their covariance a positive product a negative product nothing it depends on the units Why do we usually report correlations rather than covariances? Correlations are always positive Correlations do not depend on the units of the variables Covariances cannot be computed for more than two variables Correlations detect nonlinear relations Two variables have \(r\approx 0\). We can conclude that they are unrelated there is no linear relation, but there may be another kind one of them is constant there are outliers Answers 1 a. 2 b. 3 b. 2.6 Unusual combinations Back to the question we started with: which state is the most unusual? 2.6.1 Hawaii: ordinary on each variable The usual check for one variable is a boxplot. The box holds the middle half of the states; the whiskers reach out to at most 1.5 box lengths beyond it, and only states beyond the whiskers are drawn as separate points, the possible outliers. But a state can be ordinary on every variable and still unusual as a combination. Take two measures of education, illiteracy and the share of adults with a high-school diploma: fig_unusual <- function() { st2 <- states |> mutate(dm = dmU, hi = state == "Hawaii") z_long <- as_tibble(scale(X6[, vU])) |> mutate(state = states$state) |> pivot_longer(-state, names_to = "variable", values_to = "z") |> mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = vU, labels = c("Illiteracy", "HS grad"))) p_box <- ggplot(z_long, aes(variable, z)) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.45, outlier.shape = 1, fill = "grey95") + geom_point(data = dplyr::filter(z_long, state == "Hawaii"), colour = col_a2, size = 3.5) + annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 1.55, label = "Hawaii", colour = col_a2, size = 4.5) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-2.5, 3)) + labs(title = "One at a time", subtitle = "Hawaii: not an outlier", x = NULL, y = "standardised value") ell_r <- map_dfr(1:3, function(r) { e <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(SU), r) tibble(x = e[1, ] + xbU[1], y = e[2, ] + xbU[2], r = factor(r)) }) top <- dplyr::slice_max(st2, dm, n = 4) p_sc <- ggplot(st2, aes(Illiteracy, HSGrad)) + geom_path(data = ell_r, aes(x, y, group = r, linetype = r, colour = r), linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(aes(colour = hi), size = 2.4, alpha = 0.8) + geom_label_repel(data = top, aes(label = sprintf("%s (%.2f)", state, dm)), size = 3.7, seed = 1, fill = alpha("white", 0.85), label.size = 0, label.padding = 0.12, min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 0.6) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#6f7a8c", `TRUE` = col_a2, "1" = "black", "2" = "grey45", "3" = "grey65"), guide = "none") + scale_linetype_manual(values = c("1" = 1, "2" = 2, "3" = 3), guide = "none") + labs(title = "Together", subtitle = "Ellipses: Mahalanobis distance 1, 2, 3", x = "illiteracy (%)", y = "high-school graduates (%)") p_box + p_sc + plot_layout(widths = c(0.7, 1.3)) } # draw the figure fig_unusual() Hawaii’s standardised values are \(z=1.20\) for illiteracy and \(z=1.09\) for high-school graduation: about one standard deviation above average on each. That is outside the middle half of the states, but well within the whiskers, so neither boxplot flags it, and many states are as far from average (9 on illiteracy, 18 on graduation). But the two variables are strongly correlated (\(r=-0.66\)): states with high illiteracy usually have few high-school graduates. Hawaii has high illiteracy and many graduates, and in the scatterplot it sits off the tilted cloud. 2.6.2 The Mahalanobis distance The Euclidean distance from the centre, \(\lVert \mathbf x_t- ar{\mathbf x}Vert\) (Section 2.1.1), treats every direction alike. But the cloud is an ellipse: a step along its long axis is normal, the same step across its short axis is far out. The Mahalanobis distance measures distance from the centre in units of the cloud’s own shape, described by the sample covariance matrix \(S\) (Section 2.5): \[ d_t=\sqrt{(\mathbf x_t- ar{\mathbf x})'\,S^{-1}\,(\mathbf x_t- ar{\mathbf x})} . \] Compare it with the Euclidean distance from the centre, \(\sqrt{(\mathbf x_t- ar{\mathbf x})'(\mathbf x_t- ar{\mathbf x})}\): the only change is the inverse \(S^{-1}\) of the covariance matrix in the middle (the matrix with \(S^{-1}S=I\), the identity matrix; R computes it with solve(S)). It shrinks differences in directions where the cloud is wide and stretches them where it is narrow. With uncorrelated, standardised variables, \(S=I\) and \(d_t\) is just the Euclidean distance. Points with equal \(d_t\) lie on one ellipse; the one-standard-deviation ellipse is exactly \(d_t=1\), and the ellipses in the figure above are \(d_t=1,2,3\). A state on a further-out ellipse has a larger distance. Computed from the two variables of the scatterplot, the ranking matches what the figure shows: Hawaii, Alaska and Louisiana are the farthest out, all close to \(d=2.75\), followed by New Mexico. X2 <- state.x77[, c("Illiteracy", "HS Grad")] d2 <- sqrt(mahalanobis(X2, center = colMeans(X2), cov = cov(X2))) round(sort(d2, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 2) ## Hawaii Alaska Louisiana New Mexico South Carolina ## 2.76 2.76 2.73 2.48 2.06 fig_maha_rank <- function(k = 12, dist = sqrt(d2_st), xlab = "Mahalanobis distance (six variables)") { d <- tibble(state = names(dist), d = dist) |> slice_max(d, n = k) |> mutate(state = reorder(state, d)) ggplot(d, aes(d, state)) + geom_col(fill = col_a1, width = 0.7) + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", d)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.8) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) + labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) } # draw the figure fig_maha_rank(8, dist = dmU, xlab = "Mahalanobis distance (illiteracy and high-school graduates)") The three states are far out for different reasons. Louisiana has the highest illiteracy and few graduates: it lies beyond the end of the cloud, extreme on one variable but in line with the pattern. Hawaii and Alaska lie across the cloud: both have more graduates than their illiteracy would suggest. Hawaii reaches the same distance as Louisiana with values only about one standard deviation from average. By the Euclidean distance from the centre of the standardised values it would rank only 15th of the 50 states. With all six variables we can no longer draw the cloud, but the distance works the same way: d <- sqrt(mahalanobis(X, center = colMeans(X), cov = cov(X))) round(sort(d, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 1) ## Alaska Hawaii New Mexico Nevada Washington ## 4.7 4.0 3.8 3.7 3.4 fig_maha_rank <- function(k = 12, dist = sqrt(d2_st), xlab = "Mahalanobis distance (six variables)") { d <- tibble(state = names(dist), d = dist) |> slice_max(d, n = k) |> mutate(state = reorder(state, d)) ggplot(d, aes(d, state)) + geom_col(fill = col_a1, width = 0.7) + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", d)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.8) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) + labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) } # draw the figure fig_maha_rank() Alaska is the most unusual state, followed by Hawaii, New Mexico and Nevada. Alaska has the highest income and almost the most high-school graduates, yet a high murder rate, while among the other states income and education go with low murder rates. Hawaii has the highest life expectancy but also high illiteracy, again against the pattern of the other states. What makes them unusual is the combination of values. Is a distance of 4.7 actually surprising, or would some state always be that far out by chance? Answering this needs a model of where the data come from: the distribution of the random vector behind the sample, the topic of Chapter 3. Check your understanding Hawaii is unremarkable on illiteracy and on high-school graduation separately but unusual overall because its values are extreme its combination of values runs against the correlation of the other states it has missing data it is an island The Mahalanobis distance differs from the ordinary distance from the centre because it ignores the correlation between variables measures distance relative to the shape of the cloud only works with two variables uses absolute values instead of squares Answers 1 b. 2 b. 2.7 Summary A data set is an \(n	imes p\) data matrix \(\mathbf X\): a cloud of \(n\) points in \(p\)-dimensional space. It is the sample, the layer of the analysis we observe. Variables are nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio. Means, covariances and distances need numbers on a scale; categorical variables are counted, or used to colour and split plots. The type decides the plot: count tables for two categorical variables, boxplots for a categorical and a numeric one, scatterplots and scatterplot matrices for numeric ones. 3D plots are hard to read. A third variable is better shown in 2D, in a way that fits its type: a categorical one as colour (grouped scatterplot) or panels (conditioning, facet or trellis plots), a numeric one as size or a colour gradient (bubble plot). A hidden group can reverse a correlation (Simpson’s paradox). The covariance is an average product of deviations; the correlation removes the units. Both measure only straight-line association and can be driven by single points. The Mahalanobis distance measures distance relative to the shape of the cloud and finds unusual combinations: here Alaska and Hawaii. Whether they are surprising needs a model: Chapter 3. Look at the shape of the cloud before summarising it. 2.7.1 Further reading Everitt and Hothorn (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Chapter 1 (types of variables; covariances, correlations and distances) and Chapter 2 (scatterplots, the scatterplot matrix, bubble plots, three-dimensional plots and trellis graphics).

3 From Data to Distributions 3.1 Random experiments and random variables 3.2 Random vectors 3.3 From random vectors to a data matrix 3.4 Continuous random variables and vectors 3.5 Moments 3.6 Learning the distribution from data 3.7 From the reduced form to structural models 3.8 Summary

3 From Data to Distributions R code for this chapter: distributions_figures.R (data and figures) and _common.R (shared helpers). Save both in one folder and run source("distributions_figures.R"); every figure is then one function call, as shown under the Code buttons. Slides for this chapter: distributions_slides.html (opens in a new tab; use the arrow keys to move between slides). Chapter 2 stayed with the sample: the data matrix \(\mathbf X\), its plots and its summaries. It ended with a question it could not answer: Alaska is the state farthest from the centre of the cloud, but is a distance of 4.7 surprising? To answer it we need a model of where the data come from. This chapter builds that model step by step, starting from the simplest random experiment, rolling a die: a random variable turns the outcome of an experiment into a number (one die); a random vector collects several random variables from the same experiment (two dice); repeating the experiment \(n\) times produces a data matrix; the distribution of the random vector, and its moments, describe what such data look like. The distribution of the random vector behind the rows is the reduced form of Chapter 1. 3.1 Random experiments and random variables 3.1.1 Experiments, outcomes and events A random experiment is anything whose result we cannot predict exactly before it happens: rolling a die, recording tomorrow’s sales of a coffee shop, measuring the next flight’s fuel use. Probability theory needs three ingredients to describe it: An outcome \(\omega\) is one possible result of the experiment. For a die, \(\omega\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). The sample space \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes: \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). An event is a set of outcomes, such as “an even number”, \(\{2,4,6\}\). A probability \(P\) assigns each event a number between 0 and 1, with \(P(\Omega)=1\). For a fair die every outcome has probability \(1/6\), so \(P(\{2,4,6\})=3/6\). 3.1.2 Random variables A random variable \(X\) is a rule that assigns a number to every outcome: \(X(\omega)\). For one die the natural rule is “the number shown”, \(X(\omega)=\omega\). Other rules give other random variables on the same experiment, for example \(Y(\omega)=1\) if the number is even and \(0\) otherwise. We write random variables with capital letters (\(X\)) and the value they take once the experiment has been carried out with lower-case letters (\(x\)). Before the roll, \(X\) is random; after the roll, we observe a realisation, say \(x=4\). Data are always realisations. 3.1.3 The distribution of a discrete random variable The distribution of \(X\) says which values are possible and how likely they are. A random variable with a list of separate possible values (a count, the face of a die) is discrete, and its distribution can be given in two equivalent ways: the probability mass function (pmf) \(p(x)=P(X=x)\), the probability of each value. The probabilities are never negative and add up to one, \(\sum_x p(x)=1\); the cumulative distribution function (cdf) \(F(x)=P(X\le x)\), the probability of a value up to \(x\). It rises from 0 to 1, with a jump of size \(p(x)\) at every possible value. fig_die <- function() { pm <- tibble(x = 1:6, p = 1 / 6) p1 <- ggplot(pm, aes(x, p)) + geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = 0), colour = col_a1, linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(colour = col_a1, size = 3.5) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6, limits = c(0.5, 6.5)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.25), breaks = c(0, 1 / 6), labels = c("0", "1/6")) + labs(title = "Probability mass function", subtitle = expression(italic(p)(italic(x)) == italic(P)(italic(X) == italic(x))), x = expression("number shown"~italic(x)), y = expression(italic(p)(italic(x)))) cd <- tibble(x0 = c(0, 1:6), x1 = c(1:6, 7), F = (0:6) / 6) p2 <- ggplot(cd) + geom_segment(aes(x = x0, xend = x1, y = F, yend = F), colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(data = cd[-1, ], aes(x0, F), colour = col_a2, size = 2.8) + geom_point(data = cd[-7, ], aes(x1, F), colour = col_a2, size = 2.8, shape = 21, fill = "white") + annotate("segment", x = 3.5, xend = 3.5, y = 0, yend = 0.5, linetype = 3, colour = "grey40") + annotate("text", x = 0.1, y = 0.9, label = "italic(F)(3.5) == italic(P)(italic(X) <= 3.5)*' = 3/6'", parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, size = 3.8) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:7, limits = c(0, 7)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = (0:6) / 6, labels = c("0", paste0(1:5, "/6"), "1")) + labs(title = "Cumulative distribution function", subtitle = expression(italic(F)(italic(x)) == italic(P)(italic(X) <= italic(x))), x = expression(italic(x)), y = expression(italic(F)(italic(x)))) p1 + p2 } # draw the figure fig_die() For a fair die \(p(x)=1/6\) for \(x=1,\dots,6\), and \(F(3.5)=P(X\le 3.5)=P(X\in\{1,2,3\})=3/6\). The cdf is defined for every real number \(x\), not only for the possible values, which is why it is a staircase. x <- 1:6 p <- rep(1/6, 6) # pmf of a fair die cumsum(p) # cdf at 1, 2, ..., 6 ## [1] 0.1666667 0.3333333 0.5000000 0.6666667 0.8333333 1.0000000 sample(1:6, size = 10, replace = TRUE) # ten rolls: ten realisations of X ## [1] 5 2 1 1 1 5 3 3 6 1 Check your understanding For one roll of a die, the event “at least 5” is the number 5 the set of outcomes \(\{5,6\}\) the probability \(2/6\) a random variable Before a die is rolled, the number it will show is a realisation \(x\) a random variable \(X\) the sample space the cdf For a fair die, \(F(4)=P(X\le 4)\) equals \(1/6\) \(4/6\) \(4\) \(1\) Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 b. 3.2 Random vectors 3.2.1 Two dice, two random variables Now roll two dice. An outcome is a pair, \(\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2)\), for example \((3,5)\): 3 on the first die, 5 on the second. The sample space has \(6\times 6=36\) outcomes, all equally likely, each with probability \(1/36\). On this one experiment we can define several random variables. Take \[ X_1=\text{the first die},\qquad X_2=\text{the sum of both dice}. \] For the outcome \((3,5)\), \(X_1=3\) and \(X_2=8\). Collected in a column, they form a random vector: \[ X=\begin{pmatrix}X_1\\ X_2\end{pmatrix}. \] A random vector is simply several random variables measured on the same experiment. That is exactly the situation of multivariate data: each row of a data matrix records several variables for one observation. 3.2.2 Joint, marginal and conditional distributions The joint distribution of \(X\) gives the probability of each combination of values, \(p(x_1,x_2)=P(X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)\). Each of the 36 outcomes gives a different pair \((x_1,x_2)\), so every possible pair has probability \(1/36\) (blue points below). Pairs that cannot happen, such as \(X_1=1\) and \(X_2=12\), have probability 0. fig_dice_joint <- function(cond = 3) { jt <- expand_grid(d1 = 1:6, d2 = 1:6) |> mutate(x1 = d1, x2 = d1 + d2) m1 <- tibble(x1 = 1:6, p = 1 / 6) m2 <- jt |> count(x2) |> mutate(p = n / 36) p_main <- ggplot(jt, aes(x1, x2)) + annotate("rect", xmin = cond - 0.4, xmax = cond + 0.4, ymin = cond + 0.5, ymax = cond + 6.5, fill = col_a2, alpha = 0.12) + geom_point(size = 7, colour = col_a1, alpha = 0.85) + geom_text(label = "1/36", colour = "white", size = 2.3, fontface = "bold") + annotate("text", x = cond, y = cond + 7.1, label = sprintf("italic(X)[1] == %d", cond), parse = TRUE, colour = col_a2, size = 3.8) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6, limits = c(0.5, 6.5)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = 2:12, limits = c(1.5, 12.5)) + labs(x = expression(italic(X)[1]*": first die"), y = expression(italic(X)[2]*": sum of both dice")) p_top <- ggplot(m1, aes(x1, p)) + geom_col(width = 0.5, fill = "grey60") + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 6.5), breaks = NULL) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1 / 6), labels = c("0", "1/6")) + labs(x = NULL, y = expression(italic(P)(italic(X)[1]))) p_right <- ggplot(m2, aes(x2, p)) + geom_col(width = 0.5, fill = "grey60") + coord_flip() + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1.5, 12.5), breaks = NULL) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1 / 6), labels = c("0", "1/6")) + labs(x = NULL, y = expression(italic(P)(italic(X)[2]))) p_top + plot_spacer() + p_main + p_right + plot_layout(ncol = 2, widths = c(4, 1.3), heights = c(1, 4)) } # draw the figure fig_dice_joint() The marginal distribution of one variable ignores the other. It is obtained by adding the joint probabilities over the other variable: \(P(X_1=x_1)=\sum_{x_2}p(x_1,x_2)\). The grey bars show the two marginals. \(X_1\) is uniform (\(1/6\) each, six points per column), while \(X_2\) is triangular: a sum of 7 can happen in six ways, a sum of 2 or 12 in only one. The conditional distribution of \(X_2\) given \(X_1=x_1\) fixes the first die and asks about the sum. Take the column \(X_1=x_1\) (shaded for \(x_1=3\)) and rescale it so that it adds up to one: \[ P(X_2=x_2\mid X_1=x_1)=\frac{P(X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)}{P(X_1=x_1)} . \] Given \(X_1=3\), the sum is \(4,5,\dots,9\), each with probability \((1/36)/(1/6)=1/6\). The joint distribution of a random vector can also be described by its joint cdf, \(F(x_1,x_2)=P(X_1\le x_1,\;X_2\le x_2)\), the probability that both variables are at most the given values. 3.2.3 Independence Two random variables are independent if knowing one tells us nothing about the other: every conditional distribution of \(X_2\) is the same, whatever the value of \(X_1\). Equivalently, the joint probabilities are the product of the marginals, \(P(X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)=P(X_1=x_1)\,P(X_2=x_2)\) for all pairs. The two dice are independent: the second die does not care what the first one showed, and \(P(\text{first}=a,\text{second}=b)=\frac16\cdot\frac16=\frac1{36}\). But the first die and the sum are dependent: knowing \(X_1=6\) moves the possible sums up to \(7,\dots,12\). Indeed, \(P(X_1=1,X_2=12)=0\) while \(P(X_1=1)\,P(X_2=12)=\frac16\cdot\frac1{36}>0\). Dependence between variables is what multivariate analysis is about. The same definition works for continuous variables, with densities instead of probabilities: \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are independent if \(f(x_1,x_2)=f_1(x_1)\,f_2(x_2)\) (Section 3.4). It also works for whole random vectors: two random vectors are independent if everything about one is unrelated to everything about the other. That is the sense in which the rows of a random sample are independent (Section 3.3).
