To get data, we repeat the experiment \(n\) times. Repetition \(t\) has its own random vector, written in bold as for the rows of the data matrix in Chapter 2: \(\mathbf X_t=(X_{t1},X_{t2})'\). A plain subscript keeps indexing the variables: \(X_1\) is the first die, the bold \(\mathbf X_1\) the whole first repetition. Once repetition \(t\) has been carried out we record its realisation \(\mathbf x_t\) as row \(t\) of the data matrix, with entries \(x_{tj}\): \[ \begin{array}{ccc} \mathbf X_1,\;\mathbf X_2,\;\dots,\;\mathbf X_n & \quad\longrightarrow\quad & \mathbf X=\begin{pmatrix}x_{11}&x_{12}\\ x_{21}&x_{22}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ x_{n1}&x_{n2}\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf x_1'\\ \mathbf x_2'\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf x_n'\end{pmatrix}\\[4pt] \text{random vectors (before)} & & \text{realisations: the data (after)} \end{array} \] The simplest and most important case is a random sample: the repetitions are carried out the same way and do not influence each other. Then \(\mathbf X_1,\dots,\mathbf X_n\) are identically distributed: every row comes from the same distribution, and independent: one row tells us nothing about another. We say the rows are iid (independent and identically distributed). Here are 10 rows of the two-dice data: set.seed(1) n <- 10 d1 <- sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE) # first die, n times d2 <- sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE) # second die, n times X <- cbind(first = d1, sum = d1 + d2) # the n x 2 data matrix X ## first sum ## [1,] 1 2 ## [2,] 4 9 ## [3,] 1 6 ## [4,] 2 4 ## [5,] 5 11 ## [6,] 3 9 ## [7,] 6 8 ## [8,] 2 3 ## [9,] 3 8 ## [10,] 3 8 In a random sample the index \(t\) no longer distinguishes any distributions: every \(\mathbf X_t\) has the same distribution as the random vector \(X\) of a single experiment. So there is really only one random vector, and the data matrix is \(n\) independent draws of the same random vector \(X\), rather than one draw each of \(n\) different random vectors. When we speak of “the distribution”, its mean \(\mu=E[X]\) or its covariance matrix \(\Sigma=\operatorname{Var}(X)\), we mean those of this one \(X\); the index \(t\) is needed only to point at a particular row. Whether real data are like this is an assumption, which Section 3.6.4 questions. 3.3.2 What the data reveal about the distribution The data matrix is not the distribution, but with many iid rows it comes to look like it. Below, each blue bubble shows the share of the \(n\) rows with that pair \((x_1,x_2)\); the open circles show the probability \(1/36\). With 36 rows the shares are rough, some pairs never appear and others appear three times; with 3,600 rows they match the probabilities closely. fig_dice_sample <- function(ns = c(36, 360, 3600)) { set.seed(6350) rel <- purrr::map_dfr(ns, function(n) { d1 <- sample(1:6, n, TRUE); d2 <- sample(1:6, n, TRUE) tibble(x1 = d1, x2 = d1 + d2) |> count(x1, x2) |> mutate(f = n / !!n, n_lab = paste("n =", format(!!n, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE))) }) |> mutate(n_lab = factor(n_lab, levels = paste("n =", format(ns, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)))) truth <- expand_grid(x1 = 1:6, d2 = 1:6) |> mutate(x2 = x1 + d2, f = 1 / 36) ggplot(rel, aes(x1, x2)) + geom_point(data = truth, aes(size = f), shape = 21, colour = "grey40", fill = NA) + geom_point(aes(size = f), colour = col_a1, alpha = 0.7) + scale_size_area(max_size = 9, guide = "none") + facet_wrap(~ n_lab) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 12, 2)) + labs(x = expression(italic(x)[1]*": first die"), y = expression(italic(x)[2]*": sum"), subtitle = expression("Blue: share of the"~italic(n)~"rows at each ("*italic(x)[1]*","~italic(x)[2]*"). Circles: the probability 1/36.")) } # draw the figure fig_dice_sample() This is the idea behind all of statistics: the distribution of \(X\) is unknown, but because the rows are draws from it, the data matrix tells us more and more about it as \(n\) grows. Section 3.6 makes this precise. Check your understanding In a data matrix produced by rolling two dice \(n\) times, row \(t\) is the random vector \(\mathbf X_t\) a realisation \(\mathbf x_t\) of the random vector \(\mathbf X_t\) the joint distribution the sample space “Identically distributed” means that all rows have the same values all rows are draws from the same distribution the variables in a row are independent the data matrix is square With two dice, \(X_2\) and \(\mathbf X_2\) denote the same thing the sum of the dice, and the random vector of the second roll of both dice the second roll, and the sum of the dice the second die, twice Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 b. 3.4 Continuous random variables and vectors 3.4.1 Densities Dice have a few separate values. Many variables can take any value in a range: daily sales in dollars, flight time, fuel. Such a random variable is continuous. The probability of any single exact value is zero (\(P(X=1200.000\ldots)=0\)), so a pmf no longer works. Instead, a continuous random variable has a probability density function (pdf) \(f(x)\ge 0\): probabilities are areas under it, \[ P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1 . \] The cdf is defined exactly as before, \(F(x)=P(X\le x)\): the area to the left of \(x\). Now it is a smooth curve instead of a staircase, and the pdf is its slope, \(f(x)=F'(x)\). Here are the daily sales of a coffee shop: fig_cont_pdf_cdf <- function(x0 = 1500) { sc <- 1200 / 4 g <- tibble(x = seq(0, 4000, length.out = 400)) |> mutate(f = dgamma(x, 4, scale = sc), F = pgamma(x, 4, scale = sc)) F0 <- pgamma(x0, 4, scale = sc) p1 <- ggplot(g, aes(x, f)) + geom_area(data = dplyr::filter(g, x <= x0), fill = col_a1, alpha = 0.35) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + annotate("text", x = 650, y = 0.00018, label = sprintf("area = %.2f", F0), colour = col_a1, size = 4.2) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) + scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL) + labs(title = "Probability density function", subtitle = expression("probability = area under"~italic(f)), x = expression("daily sales"~italic(x)), y = expression(italic(f)(italic(x)))) p2 <- ggplot(g, aes(x, F)) + geom_line(colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1.1) + annotate("segment", x = x0, xend = x0, y = 0, yend = F0, linetype = 3) + annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = x0, y = F0, yend = F0, linetype = 3) + annotate("point", x = x0, y = F0, colour = col_a2, size = 3) + annotate("text", x = x0 + 120, y = F0 - 0.06, label = sprintf("italic(F)(1500) == %.2f", F0), parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, size = 4.2) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) + labs(title = "Cumulative distribution function", subtitle = expression(italic(F)(italic(x)) == italic(P)(italic(X) <= italic(x))*" = area to the left of "*italic(x)), x = expression("daily sales"~italic(x)), y = expression(italic(F)(italic(x)))) p1 + p2 } # draw the figure fig_cont_pdf_cdf() The probability that tomorrow’s sales are at most $1,500 is the shaded area, \(F(1500)=0.73\). A density value is not a probability: \(f(x)\) is large where values are crowded, and only the area over an interval is a probability. pgamma(1500, shape = 4, scale = 300) # F(1500) ## [1] 0.7349741 pgamma(1500, shape = 4, scale = 300) - pgamma(1000, shape = 4, scale = 300) # P(1000 <= X <= 1500) ## [1] 0.3079601 3.4.2 Two continuous variables: the multivariate normal For a continuous random vector the joint density \(f(x_1,x_2)\) is a surface above the plane, and probabilities are volumes under it. The most important example is the multivariate normal distribution. Take the flights of Chapter 1: \(X_1\) is the flight time and \(X_2\) the fuel burned on a random flight, both measured as deviations from the typical flight, so both have mean zero. They are dependent: longer flights burn more fuel. Their joint density is the hill below (drag to rotate): fig_normal_3d <- function(height = NULL) { gx <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 70) fz <- outer(gx, gx, function(a, b) mvtnorm::dmvnorm(cbind(a, b), sigma = air_Sigma)) p <- plot_ly(x = gx, y = gx, z = t(fz), type = "surface", colorscale = "Viridis", showscale = FALSE, contours = list(z = list(show = TRUE, usecolormap = TRUE, project = list(z = TRUE)))) |> layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "flight time X₁"), yaxis = list(title = "fuel X₂"), zaxis = list(title = "density", showticklabels = FALSE), camera = list(eye = list(x = 1.7, y = -1.8, z = 1.1)), aspectratio = list(x = 1, y = 1, z = 0.7)), margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 10, b = 0)) if (!is.null(height)) p$height <- height p } # draw the figure fig_normal_3d() A random vector with \(p\) variables is multivariate normal, \(X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)\), if its density is \[ f(x)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12\,(x-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\Big), \] where \(\mu\) is a \(p\times 1\) vector and \(\Sigma\) a symmetric \(p\times p\) matrix, and \(|\Sigma|\) is its determinant. Section 3.5 shows that \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) are the mean vector and covariance matrix: the whole hill is described by where it stands (\(\mu\)) and its shape (\(\Sigma\)). For the flights, \(\mu=(0,0)'\) and \(\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1.48&1.70\\ 1.70&3.13\end{pmatrix}\). 3.4.3 From 3D to 2D: the contour plot As we saw in Section 2.4, 3D pictures are hard to read on a flat page. The standard alternative is to look at the hill from above and draw lines of equal height, like the elevation lines (contours) on a hiking map. This is a contour plot: the 2D version of the 3D surface. fig_normal_contour <- function(points = TRUE) { gx <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 160) grid <- expand_grid(x = gx, y = gx) |> mutate(z = mvtnorm::dmvnorm(cbind(x, y), sigma = air_Sigma)) p <- ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, z = z)) + geom_contour_filled(bins = 8) + geom_contour(bins = 8, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) + scale_fill_viridis_d(guide = "none") if (points) { set.seed(7) pts <- as_tibble(mvtnorm::rmvnorm(200, sigma = air_Sigma), .name_repair = ~ c("x", "y")) p <- p + geom_point(data = pts, aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "white", alpha = 0.7, size = 1) } p + coord_equal(xlim = c(-4, 4), ylim = c(-4, 4), expand = FALSE) + labs(x = expression("flight time"~italic(X)[1]), y = expression("fuel"~italic(X)[2])) } # draw the figure fig_normal_contour() Brighter regions are higher, and that is where most of the 200 simulated flights (white dots) fall. The exponent of the normal density is \(-\tfrac12 d^2\), where \(d^2=(x-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\) is the squared Mahalanobis distance of Section 2.6.2. So equal height means equal Mahalanobis distance, and every contour is an ellipse. 3.4.4 How much probability inside each ellipse? Because the density depends on \(x\) only through \(d^2\), we can ask how likely a draw is to land inside the ellipse \(d=1\), \(d=2\) or \(d=3\). If \(X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)\) with \(p\) variables, the squared Mahalanobis distance of a draw follows a chi-square distribution with \(p\) degrees of freedom: \[ d^2=(X-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(X-\mu)\;\sim\;\chi^2_p . \] With two variables, 39% of all draws fall within \(d=1\), 86% within \(d=2\) and 98.9% within \(d=3\): fig_chisq_share <- function() { set.seed(61) n_c <- 2000 Xs <- mvtnorm::rmvnorm(n_c, sigma = air_Sigma) d2s <- mahalanobis(Xs, center = c(0, 0), cov = air_Sigma) band_lab <- cut(sqrt(d2s), c(0, 1, 2, 3, Inf), labels = c("d < 1", "1 to 2", "2 to 3", "d > 3")) shares <- round(100 * as.numeric(table(band_lab)) / n_c, 1) pal4 <- c("d < 1" = "#1f77b4", "1 to 2" = "#7b4fb5", "2 to 3" = "#ff7f0e", "d > 3" = "#d62728") ell <- purrr::map_dfr(1:3, function(c0) { e <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(air_Sigma), c0); tibble(c = c0, x1 = e[1, ], x2 = e[2, ]) }) ggplot(tibble(x1 = Xs[, 1], x2 = Xs[, 2], band = band_lab), aes(x1, x2, colour = band)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) + geom_path(data = ell, aes(x1, x2, group = c), colour = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal4, name = NULL, labels = sprintf("%s (%.1f%%)", levels(band_lab), shares)) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-5, 5), ylim = c(-5, 5)) + guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(x = expression("flight time"~italic(X)[1]), y = expression("fuel"~italic(X)[2])) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 10)) + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) } # draw the figure fig_chisq_share() So a distance is surprising if it is far out in the tail of \(\chi^2_p\). Section 3.6.5 uses this to answer the question about Alaska. 3.4.5 Marginal and conditional densities The ideas of Section 3.2 carry over, with sums replaced by integrals: the marginal density of \(X_1\) integrates the joint density over \(x_2\), \(f_1(x_1)=\int f(x_1,x_2)\,dx_2\). For the multivariate normal every marginal is again normal: flight time alone is \(N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)\); the conditional density of \(X_2\) given \(X_1=x_1\) is a slice through the hill at \(x_1\), rescaled to have area one: \(f(x_2\mid x_1)=f(x_1,x_2)/f_1(x_1)\). For the normal distribution the slices are simple: each one is again normal, its centre lies on a straight line in \(x_1\), and its spread does not depend on \(x_1\): fig_conditional <- function() { beta <- air_Sigma[1, 2] / air_Sigma[1, 1] sd_c <- sqrt(air_Sigma[2, 2] - air_Sigma[1, 2]^2 / air_Sigma[1, 1]) at <- c(-2, 0, 2) slices <- purrr::map_dfr(at, function(a) { y <- seq(beta * a - 2.8 * sd_c, beta * a + 2.8 * sd_c, length.out = 150) tibble(at = a, x2 = y, x1 = a + 1.3 * dnorm(y, beta * a, sd_c)) }) ell <- purrr::map_dfr(1:3, function(c0) { e <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(air_Sigma), c0); tibble(c = c0, x1 = e[1, ], x2 = e[2, ]) }) ggplot() + geom_path(data = ell, aes(x1, x2, group = c), colour = "grey55") + geom_segment(data = tibble(at = at), aes(x = at, xend = at, y = beta * at - 2.8 * sd_c, yend = beta * at + 2.8 * sd_c), colour = "grey65", linetype = 3) + geom_path(data = slices, aes(x1, x2, group = at), colour = col_a1, linewidth = 1.1) + geom_abline(slope = beta, intercept = 0, colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1.1) + annotate("label", x = 2.3, y = -4, label = sprintf("italic(E)*'['*italic(X)[2]~'|'~italic(X)[1]*' = '*italic(x)[1]*']' == %.2f*italic(x)[1]", beta), parse = TRUE, colour = col_a2, size = 4, label.size = 0) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.5, 4.5), ylim = c(-5, 5)) + labs(x = expression("flight time"~italic(X)[1]), y = expression("fuel"~italic(X)[2])) } # draw the figure fig_conditional() The blue curves are the conditional densities of fuel for three flight times. Their centres lie on the line \(E[X_2\mid X_1=x_1]\), the regression line. So linear regression is one conditional distribution of the joint distribution, read in one direction. As Chapter 1 argued, it does not tell us which forces moved time and fuel in the first place. How strongly the variables depend on each other sets the shape of the ellipses. Move the slider to change the correlation \(\rho\) (defined in Section 3.5) of two standardised normal variables: jump_buttons <- function(labels, frames) lapply(seq_along(labels), function(i) list( label = labels[i], method = "animate", args = list(list(frames[i]), list(mode = "immediate", frame = list(duration = 0, redraw = TRUE), transition = list(duration = 0))))) fig_rho_slider <- function() { set.seed(51) E <- matrix(rnorm(600), ncol = 2) rho_grid <- round(c(-0.95, seq(-0.9, 0.9, by = 0.1), 0.95), 2) rl <- function(r) sprintf("%.2f", r) pts_r <- purrr::map_dfr(rho_grid, function(r) { A <- matrix(c(1, 0, r, sqrt(1 - r^2)), 2, byrow = TRUE); X <- E %*% t(A) tibble(id = seq_len(nrow(X)), x1 = X[, 1], x2 = X[, 2], k = rl(r)) }) ell_r <- purrr::map_dfr(rho_grid, function(r) { S <- matrix(c(1, r, r, 1), 2) purrr::map_dfr(1:3, function(c0) { e <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(S), c0); tibble(x1 = c(e[1, ], NA), x2 = c(e[2, ], NA)) }) |> mutate(k = rl(r)) }) reg_r <- purrr::map_dfr(rho_grid, function(r) tibble(x1 = c(-4, 4), x2 = r * c(-4, 4), k = rl(r))) txt_r <- tibble(x1 = -3.9, x2 = 3.9, k = rl(rho_grid), text = sprintf("E[X<sub>2</sub> | X<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>] = %.2f x<sub>1</sub><br>Var(X<sub>2</sub> | X<sub>1</sub>) = %.2f", rho_grid, 1 - rho_grid^2)) plot_ly() |> add_trace(data = pts_r, x = ~x1, y = ~x2, frame = ~k, ids = ~id, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 5, color = "#6f7a8c", opacity = 0.5), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE) |> add_trace(data = ell_r, x = ~x1, y = ~x2, frame = ~k, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = "black", width = 1.6), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE) |> add_trace(data = reg_r, x = ~x1, y = ~x2, frame = ~k, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = col_a2, width = 2.5), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE) |> add_trace(data = txt_r, x = ~x1, y = ~x2, frame = ~k, text = ~text, type = "scatter", mode = "text", textposition = "bottom right", textfont = list(size = 13, color = "#2c3e50"), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE) |> layout(xaxis = list(title = "x<sub>1</sub>", range = c(-4, 4), zeroline = FALSE), yaxis = list(title = "x<sub>2</sub>", range = c(-4, 4), scaleanchor = "x", zeroline = FALSE), margin = list(l = 60, r = 20, t = 50, b = 60)) |> animation_opts(frame = 150, transition = 0, redraw = TRUE) |> animation_button(x = 0, xanchor = "left", y = -0.12, yanchor = "top", label = "Play") |> animation_slider(x = 0.12, len = 0.88) |> finalize_animation(jump_buttons(c("ρ = −0.8", "ρ = 0", "ρ = 0.5", "ρ = 0.9"), rl(c(-0.8, 0, 0.5, 0.9))), start_frame = "0.50", prefix = "correlation ρ = ") } # draw the figure fig_rho_slider() At \(\rho=0\) the contours are circles and the variables are independent. As \(|\rho|\) approaches one the ellipses become thin, and the points almost lie on a line. 3.4.6 Not every distribution is one hill Data need not look normal. For a cloud of points we can estimate the density directly, with a kernel density estimate: put a small smooth bump on every observation and add them up. Here is the result for the penguins’ bill length and depth (drag to rotate): fig_kde_3d <- function(height = NULL) { p <- plot_ly(x = peng_kde$x, y = peng_kde$y, z = t(peng_kde$z), type = "surface", colorscale = list(c(0, "#f7fbff"), c(0.3, "#9ecae1"), c(0.7, "#2171b5"), c(1, "#08306b")), showscale = FALSE, contours = list(z = list(show = TRUE, usecolormap = TRUE, project = list(z = TRUE)))) |> layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "bill length X₁"), yaxis = list(title = "bill depth X₂"), zaxis = list(title = "density", showticklabels = FALSE), camera = list(eye = list(x = -1.2, y = -1.9, z = 1.2)), aspectratio = list(x = 1.2, y = 1, z = 0.6)), margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 10, b = 0)) if (!is.null(height)) p$height <- height p } # draw the figure fig_kde_3d() There are three peaks. A normal distribution has only one. Drawn as a contour plot and coloured by species, the three hills turn out to be the three species: fig_kde_contour <- function(colour_species = FALSE) { p <- ggplot() + geom_contour_filled(data = peng_kde$df, aes(x, y, z = z), bins = 9, alpha = 0.85) + scale_fill_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("white", "#c6dbef", "#6baed6", "#2171b5", "#08306b"))(9), guide = "none") p <- if (colour_species) { p + geom_point(data = peng, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal_species, name = NULL) + theme(legend.position = c(0.86, 0.9), legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA)) } else { p + geom_point(data = peng, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm), colour = "grey20", size = 0.9, alpha = 0.6) } p + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(31, 61), ylim = c(13, 22), expand = FALSE) + labs(x = "bill length (mm)", y = "bill depth (mm)") } # draw the figure fig_kde_contour(colour_species = TRUE) The density found the groups without being told the species. A density with several hills is often a mixture of groups, each with its own distribution: the starting point of cluster analysis. library(palmerpenguins) peng <- na.omit(penguins) k <- MASS::kde2d(peng$bill_length_mm, peng$bill_depth_mm, n = 100) contour(k$x, k$y, k$z, xlab = "bill length (mm)", ylab = "bill depth (mm)") Check your understanding For a continuous random variable, \(P(a\le X\le b)\) is the height \(f(b)-f(a)\) the area under the density between \(a\) and \(b\) always zero the mean of \(X\) between \(a\) and \(b\) The contours of a bivariate normal density are straight lines ellipses, the sets of equal Mahalanobis distance circles, whatever the correlation parabolas For a bivariate normal, the conditional mean \(E[X_2\mid X_1=x_1]\) is constant a straight line in \(x_1\) a parabola in \(x_1\) undefined A density with three separate peaks suggests a normal distribution with high correlation a mixture of three groups measurement error too few observations Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 b. 4 b. 3.5 Moments A distribution contains a lot of information. Moments summarise it in a few numbers. They are the population versions of the sample summaries of Section 2.5. Moments are defined in the same way for every distribution; only the arithmetic differs. For a discrete distribution we add up values weighted by the pmf; for a continuous one we integrate against the pdf. To keep the two apart, this section always uses two examples side by side: Discrete (pmf, sums) Continuous (pdf, integrals) one variable one die daily sales of the coffee shop two variables two dice: first die \(X_1\), sum \(X_2\) flights: flight time \(X_1\), fuel \(X_2\) (normal) 3.5.1 Expected value and variance The expected value (mean) of a random variable is the probability-weighted average of its values, and the variance the expected squared distance from the mean: \[ \begin{array}{lll} & \text{discrete} & \text{continuous}\\[2pt] \mu=E[X] & =\sum_x x\,p(x) & =\int x\,f(x)\,dx\\[4pt] \sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X)=E\big[(X-\mu)^2\big] & =\sum_x (x-\mu)^2\,p(x) & =\int (x-\mu)^2 f(x)\,dx \end{array} \] The standard deviation is \(\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}\), in the units of \(X\). fig_moments_pair <- function() { mu_d <- 3.5; sd_d <- sqrt(35 / 12) p_d <- ggplot(tibble(x = 1:6, p = 1 / 6), aes(x, p)) + geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = 0), colour = "grey40", linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(colour = "grey25", size = 3.2) + geom_vline(xintercept = mu_d, colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1) + annotate("segment", x = mu_d - sd_d, xend = mu_d + sd_d, y = 0.06, yend = 0.06, colour = col_a1, linewidth = 1.2, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) + annotate("text", x = mu_d + 0.08, y = 0.235, label = "μ = 3.5", colour = col_a2, hjust = 0, size = 4.4) + annotate("text", x = mu_d, y = 0.085, label = "μ ± σ, σ = 1.71", colour = col_a1, size = 4) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6, limits = c(0.5, 6.5)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.25), breaks = c(0, 1 / 6), labels = c("0", "1/6")) + labs(title = "Discrete: one die", subtitle = "pmf: probabilities are heights", x = expression("number shown"~italic(x)), y = expression(italic(p)(italic(x)))) dens <- tibble(x = seq(0, 4000, length.out = 400)) |> mutate(f = dgamma(x, coffee_k, scale = mu_A / coffee_k)) ytop <- max(dens$f) p_c <- ggplot(dens, aes(x, f)) + geom_area(fill = "grey90") + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = mu_A, colour = col_a2, linewidth = 1) + annotate("segment", x = mu_A - sd_A, xend = mu_A + sd_A, y = 0.25 * ytop, yend = 0.25 * ytop, colour = col_a1, linewidth = 1.2, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) + annotate("text", x = mu_A + 60, y = 1.08 * ytop, label = "μ = $1,200", colour = col_a2, hjust = 0, size = 4.4) + annotate("text", x = mu_A, y = 0.36 * ytop, label = "μ ± σ, σ = $600", colour = col_a1, size = 4) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) + labs(title = "Continuous: daily sales", subtitle = "pdf: probabilities are areas", x = expression("daily sales"~italic(x)), y = expression(italic(f)(italic(x)))) p_d + p_c + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1)) } # draw the figure fig_moments_pair() One die. \(E[X]=(1+2+\dots+6)/6=3.5\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\big[(1-3.5)^2+\dots+(6-3.5)^2\big]/6=35/12\approx2.92\), so \(\sigma\approx1.71\). The value 3.5 is never rolled: the mean is the balance point of the distribution, not a typical value. Daily sales. The integrals give \(\mu=\$1{,}200\) and \(\sigma=\$600\). The mean lies to the right of the peak, pulled by the long right tail of high-sales days. 3.5.2 Covariance and correlation For two random variables, the covariance is the expected product of their deviations from the means, and the correlation divides out the units: \[ \sigma_{12}=\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=E\big[(X_1-\mu_1)(X_2-\mu_2)\big],\qquad \rho_{12}=\frac{\sigma_{12}}{\sigma_1\,\sigma_2}\in[-1,1] . \] The expectation is again a sum over the joint pmf or an integral over the joint pdf: \(\sigma_{12}=\sum_{x_1}\sum_{x_2}(x_1-\mu_1)(x_2-\mu_2)\,p(x_1,x_2)\) in the discrete case and \(\sigma_{12}=\iint (x_1-\mu_1)(x_2-\mu_2)\,f(x_1,x_2)\,dx_1\,dx_2\) in the continuous case. Two dice. The sum is the first die plus an independent second die, so the two move together exactly as much as the first die moves on its own: \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=35/12\). The sum has twice the variance of one die, \(35/6\), so \(\rho_{12}=(35/12)/\sqrt{(35/12)(35/6)}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.71\). Flights. Flight time has variance \(\sigma_1^2=1.48\), fuel \(\sigma_2^2=3.13\), and their covariance is \(\sigma_{12}=1.70\), so \(\rho_{12}=1.70/\sqrt{1.48\cdot3.13}\approx0.79\): longer flights burn more fuel. 3.5.3 Mean vector and covariance matrix For a random vector \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_p)'\), the means form the mean vector and the variances and covariances the covariance matrix: \[ \mu=E[X]=\begin{pmatrix}\mu_1\\ \vdots\\ \mu_p\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Sigma=E\big[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)'\big]= \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_1^2&\cdots&\sigma_{1p}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \sigma_{p1}&\cdots&\sigma_p^2\end{pmatrix}. \] Collecting the numbers above: \[ \text{two dice:}\quad \mu=\begin{pmatrix}3.5\\7\end{pmatrix},\quad \Sigma=\frac{35}{12}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}; \qquad\qquad \text{flights:}\quad \mu=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1.48&1.70\\ 1.70&3.13\end{pmatrix}. \] Geometrically, \(\mu\) is the centre of the distribution and \(\Sigma\) its shape, drawn as the one-standard-deviation ellipse (red diamond and black ellipse below). For the dice the ellipse summarises 36 separate points; for the flights it summarises a smooth hill. For the multivariate normal the summary is complete: the parameters \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) in its density (Section 3.4) are exactly its mean vector and covariance matrix, so the two moments describe the whole distribution. For the dice they do not: many different distributions share the same \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\). fig_mean_cov_pair <- function() { S_d <- 35 / 12 * matrix(c(1, 1, 1, 2), 2, 2); mu_dv <- c(3.5, 7) jt <- expand_grid(d1 = 1:6, d2 = 1:6) |> mutate(x1 = d1, x2 = d1 + d2) e_d <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(S_d), 1) p_d <- ggplot(jt, aes(x1, x2)) + geom_point(colour = "grey35", size = 2.6) + geom_path(data = tibble(x1 = e_d[1, ] + mu_dv[1], x2 = e_d[2, ] + mu_dv[2]), colour = "black", linewidth = 1) + annotate("point", x = mu_dv[1], y = mu_dv[2], colour = col_a2, size = 4.5, shape = 18) + annotate("text", x = mu_dv[1] + 0.35, y = mu_dv[2] - 0.6, label = "μ", colour = col_a2, size = 6) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = 2:12) + labs(title = "Discrete: two dice", subtitle = "joint pmf: each point has probability 1/36", x = expression(italic(X)[1]*": first die"), y = expression(italic(X)[2]*": sum")) g <- seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 120) grid <- expand_grid(x1 = g, x2 = g) |> mutate(f = mvtnorm::dmvnorm(cbind(x1, x2), sigma = air_Sigma)) e_c <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(air_Sigma), 1) p_c <- ggplot(grid, aes(x1, x2)) + geom_raster(aes(fill = f), interpolate = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "grey45") + geom_path(data = tibble(x1 = e_c[1, ], x2 = e_c[2, ]), colour = "black", linewidth = 1) + annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, colour = col_a2, size = 4.5, shape = 18) + annotate("text", x = 0.45, y = -0.6, label = "μ", colour = col_a2, size = 6) + coord_equal(expand = FALSE) + labs(title = "Continuous: flights", subtitle = "joint pdf: darker = higher density", x = expression("flight time"~italic(X)[1]~"(centred)"), y = expression("fuel"~italic(X)[2]~"(centred)")) p_d + p_c + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1)) } # draw the figure fig_mean_cov_pair() Every population moment has a sample counterpart, computed from the data matrix: Population (the distribution) Sample (the data matrix, Section 2.5) mean \(\mu=E[X]\) \(\bar{\mathbf x}=\frac1n\sum_t \mathbf x_t\) variance \(\sigma_j^2=E[(X_j-\mu_j)^2]\) \(s_j^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_t (x_{tj}-\bar x_j)^2\) covariance matrix \(\Sigma=E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)']\) \(S=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_t (\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x})(\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x})'\) correlation \(\rho_{jk}=\sigma_{jk}/(\sigma_j\sigma_k)\) \(r_{jk}=s_{jk}/(s_js_k)\) Population moments are fixed numbers, properties of the distribution. Sample moments change from sample to sample. With many draws they come close to the population values (Section 3.6 explains why): set.seed(2) n <- 10000 d1 <- sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE); d2 <- sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE) X <- cbind(first = d1, sum = d1 + d2) # dice: discrete colMeans(X) # close to (3.5, 7) ## first sum ## 3.5471 7.0413 cov(X) # close to (2.92, 2.92; 2.92, 5.83) ## first sum ## first 2.908872 2.925397 ## sum 2.925397 5.869181 F <- mvtnorm::rmvnorm(n, sigma = air_Sigma) # flights: continuous (normal) round(cov(F), 2) # close to the flights' Sigma ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 1.52 1.76 ## [2,] 1.76 3.18 3.5.4 Linear transformations Many random vectors are built from simpler ones by multiplying with a matrix and adding a constant, \(Y=a+AX\). Their moments then follow directly from those of \(X\): \[ E[Y]=a+A\,\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=A\,\Sigma\,A' . \] The second rule follows from the definition: \(Y-E[Y]=A(X-\mu)\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=E\big[A(X-\mu)(X-\mu)'A'\big]=A\,E\big[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)'\big]A'=A\Sigma A'\) (the transpose of a product reverses the order, \((AB)'=B'A'\)). Two dice. Let \(D=(D_1,D_2)'\) be the two dice. They are independent, so their covariance is zero and \(\operatorname{Var}(D)=\frac{35}{12}I\), with \(I\) the identity matrix. The first die and the sum are a linear transformation of \(D\): \[ X=\begin{pmatrix}X_1\\ X_2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}D_1\\ D_2\end{pmatrix} =AD, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=A\Big(\tfrac{35}{12}I\Big)A'=\frac{35}{12}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 1&2\end{pmatrix}, \] the covariance matrix we found by hand above. Two independent variables, combined by \(A\), have become two dependent ones. Flights. This is exactly the structural model of Chapter 1. Flight time and fuel are driven by two independent shocks, headwind and load, collected in \(\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)'\) with \(E[\varepsilon]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)=I\). The observed random vector is \(X=A\varepsilon\), so \[ E[X]=0,\qquad \Sigma=\operatorname{Var}(X)=A\,I\,A'=AA' . \] With the matrix \(A\) of the flights, \(AA'=\begin{pmatrix}1.48&1.70\\ 1.70&3.13\end{pmatrix}\), the covariance matrix of the flight distribution above. If the shocks are normal, \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,I)\), then \(X=A\varepsilon\) is again normal, \(X\sim N(0,AA')\): a linear transformation of a normal random vector is normal. The structural form (\(A\) and the distribution of \(\varepsilon\)) determines the reduced form (\(\Sigma=AA'\)). Section 3.7 returns to the reverse question. A <- matrix(c(1, 1, 0, 1), 2, 2) # first die, sum = A %*% (die 1, die 2) A %*% (35/12 * diag(2)) %*% t(A) # covariance matrix of (first die, sum) ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 2.916667 2.916667 ## [2,] 2.916667 5.833333 air_A %*% t(air_A) # flights (air_A from distributions_figures.R): Sigma = A A' ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 1.48 1.70 ## [2,] 1.70 3.13 Check your understanding The expected value of one fair die is 3 3.5 4 undefined, because 3.5 cannot be rolled For the first die \(X_1\) and the sum \(X_2\) of two dice, \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)\) equals 0, because the dice are independent the variance of one die, \(35/12\) 1 7 If \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\Sigma\) and \(Y=AX\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) equals \(A\Sigma\) \(A\Sigma A'\) \(A'\Sigma A\) \(\Sigma\) Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 b. 3.6 Learning the distribution from data The distribution of \(X\), and with it \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\), is unknown. What we have is a data matrix: \(n\) draws \(\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n\). Section 3.3 showed that with many iid draws the data come to look like the distribution; this section makes that precise for the sample moments of the table above, and then uses it to answer the question about Alaska. 3.6.1 Every sample gives a different estimate Take the coffee shop’s daily sales \(X\), with \(\mu=\$1{,}200\) and \(\sigma=\$600\) (Section 3.5). Here are 20 months, 30 days each. Every month gives a different sample mean (red diamond) and a different spread (blue bar, \(\bar x\pm s\)), scattered around the true \(\mu\) (black line). fig_sampling_var <- function() { set.seed(11) n_s <- 30; R_s <- 20 samples <- purrr::map_dfr(1:R_s, function(r) tibble(sample = r, x = rgamma(n_s, shape = coffee_k, scale = mu_A / coffee_k))) summ <- samples |> group_by(sample) |> summarise(xbar = mean(x), s = sd(x)) ggplot(samples, aes(x, factor(sample))) + geom_vline(xintercept = mu_A, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.2) + geom_segment(data = summ, aes(x = xbar - s, xend = xbar + s, y = factor(sample), yend = factor(sample)), colour = col_a1, linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.7) + geom_point(data = summ, aes(xbar, factor(sample)), colour = col_a2, size = 3, shape = 18) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) + labs(x = "daily sales", y = "month (30 days each)") } # draw the figure fig_sampling_var() Before the month starts, its days are random variables \(X_1,\dots,X_{30}\) (one variable, so plain letters), so the sample mean \(\bar X=\frac1n\sum_t X_t\) is itself a random variable, and each month gives one realisation \(\bar x\). Its distribution is the sampling distribution. How close is it to \(\mu\)? Two classic results answer this. 3.6.2 The law of large numbers The law of large numbers (LLN) says that if the rows are iid draws of \(X\), the sample mean gets arbitrarily close to the population mean as the sample grows: \[ \bar x=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n x_t\;\longrightarrow\;\mu=E[X] \qquad (n\to\infty). \] Press Play: six shops with the same distribution start far apart and are pulled toward \(\mu\). The grey band \(\mu\pm 2\sigma/\sqrt n\) shows how fast: \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n\), so the typical error shrinks with \(\sqrt n\), and four times the data halves the error. jump_buttons <- function(labels, frames) lapply(seq_along(labels), function(i) list( label = labels[i], method = "animate", args = list(list(frames[i]), list(mode = "immediate", frame = list(duration = 0, redraw = TRUE), transition = list(duration = 0))))) fig_lln <- function(height = NULL) { set.seed(21) n_lln <- 2000; paths <- 6 g <- unique(round(10^seq(0, log10(n_lln), length.out = 32))) runs <- purrr::map_dfr(1:paths, function(k) { x <- rgamma(n_lln, shape = coffee_k, scale = mu_A / coffee_k) tibble(path = paste("shop", k), n = g, m = (cumsum(x) / seq_len(n_lln))[g]) }) lln_frames <- purrr::map_dfr(g, function(nn) runs |> dplyr::filter(n <= nn) |> mutate(frame = as.character(nn))) band <- tibble(n = 10^seq(0, log10(n_lln), length.out = 200)) |> mutate(lo = mu_A - 2 * sd_A / sqrt(n), hi = mu_A + 2 * sd_A / sqrt(n)) pal6 <- c("#1f77b4", "#d62728", "#2ca02c", "#ff7f0e", "#7b4fb5", "#8c564b") fig <- plot_ly() |> add_ribbons(data = band, x = ~n, ymin = ~lo, ymax = ~hi, fillcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)", line = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0.25)", width = 1), hoverinfo = "skip", name = "μ ± 2σ/√n", inherit = FALSE) |> add_lines(x = c(1, n_lln), y = c(mu_A, mu_A), line = list(color = "black", width = 2), name = "μ = 1,200", hoverinfo = "skip", inherit = FALSE) |> add_lines(data = lln_frames, x = ~n, y = ~m, frame = ~frame, split = ~path, color = ~path, colors = pal6, line = list(width = 2), hoverinfo = "skip", inherit = FALSE, showlegend = FALSE) |> layout(xaxis = list(title = "days observed n (log scale)", type = "log"), yaxis = list(title = "running sample mean ($)", range = c(0, 3000)), legend = list(x = 0.7, y = 0.98), margin = list(l = 70, r = 20, t = 60, b = 60)) |> animation_opts(frame = 120, transition = 0, redraw = TRUE) |> animation_button(x = 0, xanchor = "left", y = -0.2, yanchor = "top", label = "Play") |> animation_slider(x = 0.12, len = 0.88) |> finalize_animation(jump_buttons(c("n = 10", "n = 100", "n = 2,000"), as.character(g[c(which.min(abs(g - 10)), which.min(abs(g - 100)), length(g))])), start_frame = as.character(g[which.min(abs(g - 10))]), prefix = "days observed: ") if (!is.null(height)) fig$height <- height fig } # draw the figure fig_lln() The same holds for the other moments: the sample covariance matrix \(S\) converges to \(\Sigma\). That is why the dice summaries in Section 3.5 came so close to \((3.5,7)'\) and \(\frac{35}{12}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), and why sample summaries can stand in for the moments of the reduced form. 3.6.3 The central limit theorem The central limit theorem (CLT) describes the shape of the sampling distribution. Daily sales are right-skewed (\(n=1\) below). The average of 3 days is less skewed, the average of 10 or 30 days is almost exactly a bell curve: fig_clt <- function() { set.seed(31) n_clt <- c(1, 3, 10, 30) clt <- purrr::map_dfr(n_clt, function(n) tibble(n = n, xbar = colMeans(matrix(rgamma(n * 10000, shape = coffee_k, scale = mu_A / coffee_k), nrow = n)))) clt_curve <- purrr::map_dfr(n_clt, function(n) tibble(n = n, x = seq(0, 4000, length.out = 300), y = dnorm(x, mu_A, sd_A / sqrt(n)))) lab_n <- function(n) factor(paste("n =", n), levels = paste("n =", n_clt)) ggplot(clt |> mutate(n = lab_n(n)), aes(xbar)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 40, fill = "grey65", colour = NA) + geom_line(data = clt_curve |> mutate(n = lab_n(n)), aes(x, y), colour = col_a1, linewidth = 1) + facet_wrap(~ n, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 3500), breaks = c(0, 1200, 2400), labels = scales::dollar) + labs(x = "sample mean of n days", y = "density") + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) } # draw the figure fig_clt() For large \(n\), \[ \bar X\;\approx\;N\!\Big(\mu,\;\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\Big), \] whatever the shape of the distribution of \(X\). The LLN says \(\bar x\) gets close to \(\mu\); the CLT says how close, with a normal distribution. This is the basis of standard errors and confidence intervals, and one reason the normal distribution appears everywhere in statistics. 3.6.4 When the rows are not identically distributed Both results need the rows to be draws of one random vector \(X\). Compare two coffee shops. Shop A has the same distribution every day. Shop B is growing: day \(t\) has its own, higher, distribution, so \(\mathbf X_t\) really does depend on \(t\). Press Play: shop A’s histogram settles on one curve (black); shop B’s has no single curve (red) to settle on. jump_buttons <- function(labels, frames) lapply(seq_along(labels), function(i) list( label = labels[i], method = "animate", args = list(list(frames[i]), list(mode = "immediate", frame = list(duration = 0, redraw = TRUE), transition = list(duration = 0))))) fig_coffee <- function(height = fig_coffee_mean() Shop A’s sample mean settles on \(\mu=\$1{,}200\). Shop B’s settles on nothing; it trails behind expected sales, which keep rising. Each day has its own mean \(\mu_t=E[X_t]\), and there is no single \(\mu\) for \(\bar x\) to estimate. So sample quantities such as \(\bar{\mathbf x}\) and \(S\) estimate \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) only if all rows share one distribution: in the language of Chapter 1, one reduced form. 3.6.5 Back to the states: is Alaska surprising? Now everything is in place for the question of Chapter 2. Treat the 50 states as iid draws of one random vector \(X\) with the six variables, and assume \(X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)\). Then, by Section 3.4.4, the squared Mahalanobis distance of each state follows a \(\chi^2_6\) distribution. We do not know \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\), so, as the LLN suggests, we replace them by \(\bar{\mathbf x}\) and \(S\): these are exactly the distances \(d_t\) of Section 2.6.2. Only 2.5% of draws should exceed the 97.5% quantile of \(\chi^2_6\), 14.4: about one state in 50. To check the whole distribution at once, not just one cut-off, we use a quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot. Sort the 50 values of \(d_t^2\); the \(k\)-th smallest is the sample’s \((k-0.5)/50\) quantile. Plot it against the same quantile of the distribution it should follow, here \(\chi^2_6\). If the data really come from that distribution, sample and theoretical quantiles agree and the points lie on the 45-degree line; points bending away from the line show where the distribution fails, and points far above it at the top right are observations more extreme than the distribution allows. The idea works for any statistic and any distribution it is supposed to follow: plot the sorted values against the matching theoretical quantiles. In R, qqnorm() does this for the normal distribution, and qqplot(qchisq(ppoints(n), df), sort(d2)) for the chi-square. A Q-Q plot against the chi-square, as here, is often called a chi-square plot. fig_state_qq <- function() { d2 <- d2_st; n <- length(d2) qq <- tibble(id = names(d2), d2 = d2) |> arrange(d2) |> mutate(q = qchisq(ppoints(n), df = 6), flag = d2 > thr6) ggplot(qq, aes(q, d2)) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey40") + geom_hline(yintercept = thr6, linetype = 2) + geom_point(aes(colour = flag), size = 2.3) + geom_text_repel(data = qq |> dplyr::slice_max(d2, n = 4), aes(label = id), size = 3.8, nudge_x = -3, direction = "y", min.segment.length = 0, seed = 1) + annotate("text", x = 0.3, y = thr6 + 0.8, hjust = 0, size = 3.6, label = sprintf("97.5%% cut-off = %.1f", thr6)) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#6f7a8c", `TRUE` = col_a2), guide = "none") + labs(x = "χ²(6) quantile", y = "ordered squared Mahalanobis distance") } # draw the figure fig_state_qq() X <- state.x77[, c("Income", "Illiteracy", "Life Exp", "Murder", "HS Grad", "Frost")] d2 <- mahalanobis(X, center = colMeans(X), cov = cov(X)) cutoff <- qchisq(0.975, df = ncol(X)) round(cutoff, 1) ## [1] 14.4 round(sort(d2[d2 > cutoff], decreasing = TRUE), 1) ## Alaska Hawaii ## 21.9 15.9 qqplot(qchisq(ppoints(50), df = 6), d2, # the Q-Q plot in base R xlab = "chi-square(6) quantile", ylab = "ordered squared distance"); abline(0, 1) Alaska and Hawaii exceed the cut-off, with New Mexico and Nevada close. So the answer is yes: a distance of 4.7 is surprising, if the assumptions hold. Each of them can be questioned, and each was a topic of this chapter: one distribution (Section 3.6.4): Alaska and Hawaii might well follow a different one; normality (Section 3.4): the probabilities come from the normal distribution; estimated moments (the LLN): with only 50 states, \(\bar{\mathbf x}\) and \(S\) are estimates, and they are themselves pulled toward the unusual states. Check your understanding To halve the typical error of a sample mean, we need twice as many observations four times as many observations half as many observations a normal distribution The central limit theorem says that daily sales are normally distributed the sample mean is approximately normal for large \(n\), whatever the distribution of the data the sample mean equals \(\mu\) for large \(n\) the variance of the data shrinks with \(n\) Why does shop B’s sample mean not settle on a single value? The sample is too small Sales are skewed Every day comes from a different distribution The mean does not exist for sales data If \(X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)\) with \(p=6\) variables, the squared Mahalanobis distance follows a normal distribution a \(\chi^2\) distribution with 6 degrees of freedom a uniform distribution a \(\chi^2\) distribution with 50 degrees of freedom In a Q-Q plot of the squared Mahalanobis distances against \(\chi^2_6\), points far above the line at the top right indicate observations that are more unusual than the normal distribution predicts a perfect fit negative correlation missing values Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 c. 4 b. 5 a. 3.7 From the reduced form to structural models Everything in this chapter, distributions, moments, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, describes the observed random vector \(X\): the reduced form. Its mean \(\mu\) and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) can be estimated from data, and with enough data they are known well. Often, though, we are interested in the structural parameters behind it: the hidden forces that move the variables together. In Chapter 1 these were the shocks \(\varepsilon\) and the matrix \(A\) in \[ X=A\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,I)\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad X\sim N(0,\Sigma),\quad \Sigma=AA' \] (Section 3.5.4). The structural form determines the reduced form. Can we go back, from \(\Sigma\) to \(A\)? Not uniquely. Take any rotation matrix \(Q\); with two variables, turning by an angle \(\varphi\), \[ Q=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi&-\sin\varphi\\ \sin\varphi&\cos\varphi\end{pmatrix},\qquad QQ'=I . \] Then \(\tilde A=AQ\) implies the same covariance matrix, \[ \tilde A\tilde A'=AQ\,Q'A'=A\,I\,A'=AA'=\Sigma . \] In fact the two structural models are indistinguishable, not just equal in \(\Sigma\): with \(\tilde\varepsilon=Q'\varepsilon\) we have \(X=A\varepsilon=AQQ'\varepsilon=\tilde A\tilde\varepsilon\), and \(\tilde\varepsilon\sim N(0,Q'IQ)=N(0,I)\) is again a pair of independent standard normal shocks. Both stories produce exactly the same distribution of \(X\), so no amount of data can tell them apart. This is what the slider in Section 1.3 showed: turning the two arrows (the columns of \(A\)) by \(\varphi\) keeps both tips on the same ellipse, and every angle fits the flights perfectly. The counting is the same in general. With \(p\) variables, \(\Sigma\) has \(p(p+1)/2\) distinct entries, \(A\) has \(p^2\), and the difference, \(p(p-1)/2\), is the number of free angles of a rotation. With \(p=2\): three numbers in \(\Sigma\), four in \(A\), one free angle \(\varphi\). Sigma <- air_A %*% t(air_A) phi <- pi / 6 # any angle Q <- matrix(c(cos(phi), sin(phi), -sin(phi), cos(phi)), 2, 2) A_rot <- air_A %*% Q # a different structural matrix round(A_rot %*% t(A_rot) - Sigma, 10) # same Sigma: zero matrix ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0 0 ## [2,] 0 0 Choosing one \(A\), that is, one angle, requires an extra restriction that does not come from the data: this is identification. Section 1.4 showed four such restrictions for the same cloud, each natural in a different application: the symmetric root (\(A=A'\)), Cholesky (\(a_{12}=0\), the regression ordering), PCA (the first column as long as possible) and a known coefficient from outside the data (the manual’s fuel flow). Each method in the coming chapters is a structural model of this kind: it maps the reduced form to structural parameters with its own identifying assumptions. fig_roadmap <- function() { boxes <- tibble( x = c(0.9, 3.2, 6.2, 6.2, 6.2, 6.2, 6.2), y = c(0, 0, 2.4, 1.2, 0, -1.2, -2.4), w = c(1.5, 1.9, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), title = c("Sample", "Reduced form", "PCA", "MDS", "Factor analysis", "Cluster analysis", "CFA and SEM"), sub = c("data matrix 𝐗", "𝑋: μ, Σ", "shocks ordered by variance", "coordinates from distances", "few common factors + unique shocks", "discrete latent groups", "restrictions from theory"), fill = c("#fdebd5", "#d9f2ec", rep("#f5dfeb", 5))) ggplot(boxes) + geom_rect(aes(xmin = x - w / 2, xmax = x + w / 2, ymin = y - 0.45, ymax = y + 0.45, fill = I(fill)), colour = "grey40") + geom_text(aes(x, y + 0.17, label = title), fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) + geom_text(aes(x, y - 0.12, label = sub), size = 3.4) + annotate("segment", x = 1.7, xend = 2.2, y = 0, yend = 0, colour = col_e, linewidth = 1.1, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed")) + annotate("text", x = 1.95, y = 0.25, label = "infer", colour = col_e, fontface = "bold", size = 4) + annotate("segment", x = 4.2, xend = 4.85, y = 0, yend = c(2.4, 1.2, 0, -1.2, -2.4), colour = col_h, linewidth = 0.9, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed")) + annotate("text", x = 3.2, y = 1.25, label = "identify:\nstructural models", colour = col_h, fontface = "bold", size = 4, lineheight = 0.9) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 7.7), ylim = c(-3, 3.4), expand = FALSE) + theme_void() } # draw the figure fig_roadmap() Principal components analysis (PCA, Chapter 4): orders the shocks by how much variance they explain. Multidimensional scaling (MDS, Chapter 5): recovers coordinates from distances between observations. Exploratory factor analysis (Chapter 6): a few common factors plus a unique shock for each variable. Cluster analysis (Chapter 7): discrete latent groups, like the penguin species. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation models (CFA and SEM, Chapter 8): restrictions from theory. 3.8 Summary A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of a random experiment; a random vector collects several random variables from the same experiment (the first die and the sum of two dice). Repeating the experiment \(n\) times gives random vectors \(\mathbf X_1,\dots,\mathbf X_n\); their realisations \(\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n\) are the rows of the data matrix. In a random sample the rows are iid: \(n\) independent draws of one random vector \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_p)'\). A distribution is given by a cdf \(F(x)=P(X\le x)\), and by a pmf (probabilities are heights) or a pdf (probabilities are areas). Random vectors have joint, marginal and conditional distributions. The multivariate normal is one hill with elliptical contours; its conditional means are regression lines. Densities with several hills suggest groups. Moments summarise a distribution: the mean vector \(\mu\) and the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). A linear transformation \(Y=a+AX\) has mean \(a+A\mu\) and covariance matrix \(A\Sigma A'\). Sample moments estimate the moments of \(X\). Law of large numbers: \(\bar{\mathbf x}\to\mu\) and \(S\to\Sigma\). Central limit theorem: \(\bar X\) is approximately normal, with variance \(\sigma^2/n\). Both need the rows to share one distribution, the reduced form. Under normality, \(d^2\sim\chi^2_p\): Alaska and Hawaii are surprisingly far from the centre. All of this describes the observed \(X\). Structural parameters need identification; the coming chapters, starting with PCA, are structural models with different identifying assumptions. Data are draws from a distribution. The reduced form describes that distribution; structural models try to explain it. 3.8.1 Further reading Everitt and Hothorn (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Chapter 1 (the multivariate normal density function) and Chapter 2 (the chi-square plot, bivariate densities and kernel density estimation).

4 Principal Components Analysis R code for this chapter: pca_figures.R (data and figures) and _common.R (shared helpers). Save both in one folder and run source("pca_figures.R"); every figure is then one function call, as shown under the Code buttons. Slides for this chapter: pca_slides.html (opens in a new tab; use the arrow keys to move between slides). The Introduction wrote the data as unit-variance shocks moved by a matrix, \(\mathbf x_t=A\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\), and showed that many \(A\) fit the same data. This chapter first adds one more step to that story: shocks with units. Splitting \(A\) into a part that scales the shocks and a part that combines them puts the Introduction’s choices of \(A\) (Cholesky, symmetric root, structural, PCA) into one frame (Section 4.1). The rest of the chapter works out one of them, principal components analysis (PCA): how to find the components, whether to start from the covariance or the correlation matrix, how many components to keep, how to read and use them, and what they do and do not tell us. The examples of the Introduction carry the first sections, with two variables so that every step can be drawn: education and earnings, roommates’ grades, the flights, and above all Coca-Cola and Pepsi sales. The six state indicators of Chapter 2 then show PCA with more variables. Notation as in the Introduction. Each variable is measured as a deviation from its mean, so the observations \(\mathbf x_t\) (rows of the data matrix \(\mathbf X\), bold because they are vectors) are centred, and the structural form is \[ \mathbf x_t=A\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t , \] with uncorrelated, unit-variance shocks \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) and \(AA'=\Sigma\). In the Introduction \(\Sigma\) was known. With data it is not: it is estimated by the sample covariance matrix \(S\) (Chapter 3), so the \(A\) we compute satisfies \(AA'=S\) and is an estimate too, as is everything derived from it below (to keep the formulas light, we drop the hats). 4.1 Factors with units: \(A=\Gamma D\) 4.1.1 Shocks have no units Each choice of \(A\) in the Introduction came with a story: a regression of earnings on education (Cholesky), roommates’ grades (symmetric root), the flights (a structural restriction), and Coke and Pepsi (PCA). In every story the shocks have variance one. A shock of one means “one standard deviation more than usual”, which is a convenient coordinate but not a measurement. A pilot reports headwind in km/h, a registrar reports a GPA, an economist reports years of schooling. To speak about the forces in such units, \(A\) needs one more step. 4.1.2 Scale, then combine Split \(A\) into two steps, \[ \mathbf f_t=D\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t,\qquad \mathbf x_t=\Gamma\,\mathbf f_t,\qquad\text{so}\qquad A=\Gamma D . \] \(D\) is diagonal. It scales each unit-variance shock into a factor with its own units. The factors are still uncorrelated, and their variances, the diagonal of \(D^2\), say how important each factor is. \(\Gamma\) says how the measured variables respond to one unit of each factor. The covariance matrix becomes \(S=AA'=\Gamma D^2\Gamma'\): the factor variances \(D^2\), combined by \(\Gamma\). The split is not unique. Doubling the unit of factor \(j\) (halving \(d_j\)) and doubling column \(j\) of \(\Gamma\) leaves \(A\) unchanged. So, on top of the restriction that picked \(A\), splitting it needs one more assumption per factor, a normalisation that fixes the unit in which the factor is measured. Each story of the Introduction suggests a natural one. In each figure below, the unit-variance shocks (left) are scaled by \(D\) into factors (middle), which \(\Gamma\) combines into the data (right); the arrows show what one standard deviation of each factor does, and one observation (orange) is followed through the layers. 4.1.3 Cholesky: a regression Take years of education \(x_1\) and annual earnings \(x_2\) (in $1000). The Cholesky restriction of the Introduction is \(a_{12}=0\): education does not respond to the earnings shock. With Coke and Pepsi, the slider of the Introduction finds it. 4.2.1 Every rotation fits the data Each week’s Coke and Pepsi sales (as deviations from the mean) are a combination of two uncorrelated shocks with variance one, \[ \mathbf x_t=A\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t=\varepsilon_{t1}\,a_1+\varepsilon_{t2}\,a_2 , \] where \(a_1\) and \(a_2\), the columns of \(A\), are the two arrows: what one standard deviation of each shock does to the two sales figures. Any \(A\) with \(AA'=S\) fits the data equally well (Section 1.3): turning both arrows together by an angle \(\varphi\) keeps their tips on the one-standard-deviation ellipse and leaves \(S\) unchanged. Algebraically, \(A(\varphi)=S^{1/2}Q(\varphi)\), with \(S^{1/2}\) the symmetric root and \(Q(\varphi)\) the rotation matrix of Section 3.7. 4.2.2 How much variance each arrow carries One number summarises how much the data vary in all directions together: the total variance, the sum of the variances of the variables. It is the sum of the diagonal entries of \(S\), called the trace: \[ \operatorname{tr}(S)=\operatorname{tr}\begin{pmatrix}s_1^2&s_{12}\\ s_{12}&s_2^2\end{pmatrix}=s_1^2+s_2^2 . \] The covariance \(s_{12}\) is off the diagonal and does not enter. Now write each variance in terms of the arrows. Variable 1 is \(x_{t1}=a_{11}\varepsilon_{t1}+a_{12}\varepsilon_{t2}\), and the shocks are uncorrelated with variance one, so by the rule for linear combinations (Section 3.5.4) \[ s_1^2=a_{11}^2\operatorname{var}(\varepsilon_{t1})+a_{12}^2\operatorname{var}(\varepsilon_{t2})+2a_{11}a_{12}\operatorname{cov}(\varepsilon_{t1},\varepsilon_{t2}) =a_{11}^2+a_{12}^2 , \] and in the same way \(s_2^2=a_{21}^2+a_{22}^2\). Adding the two and regrouping the four squares by shock instead of by variable, \[ \operatorname{tr}(S)=\underbrace{(a_{11}^2+a_{12}^2)}_{s_1^2}+\underbrace{(a_{21}^2+a_{22}^2)}_{s_2^2} =\underbrace{(a_{11}^2+a_{21}^2)}_{\lVert a_1\rVert^2}+\underbrace{(a_{12}^2+a_{22}^2)}_{\lVert a_2\rVert^2} . \] The first grouping splits the total variance by variable, the second by shock: \(a_{11}^2+a_{21}^2\) collects what the first shock adds to the variance of each variable, and it is the squared length of the first column of \(A\), the first arrow. The squared length of an arrow is the part of the total variance that its shock carries. The total is fixed by the data; the rotation only decides how it is divided. \(A'A=AA'=S\), so the squared arrow lengths equal the two variances, 1 and 1.1, or 48% and 52% of the total. As they turn, the blue arrow grows and the red one shrinks, until at \(\varphi\approx46\) degrees the blue arrow is as long as it can be: Principal components analysis chooses the rotation at which the first arrow is longest, so that the first shock carries as much of the total variance as possible. At that angle, \(\lVert a_1\rVert^2=2.00\), or 95% of the total, and \(\lVert a_2\rVert^2=0.10\). The two arrows are perpendicular and point along the axes of the ellipse: the long axis is the market (both brands up together), the short axis brand switching. These two directions are the principal components. With \(p\) variables there are \(p\) arrows, and the same idea continues: the first arrow as long as possible, then the second as long as possible given the first, and so on. 4.2.3 Scores: taking \(A\) apart one layer at a time Split the PCA choice of \(A\) as in Section 4.1, \[ A=\Gamma D=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma_1&\gamma_2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}d_1&0\\0&d_2\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}d_1\gamma_1&d_2\gamma_2\end{pmatrix}, \] with the columns of \(\Gamma\) of length one. Column by column, each arrow is a length times a unit-length direction: \[ a_j=d_j\,\gamma_j,\qquad d_j=\lVert a_j\rVert,\qquad \gamma_j=a_j/\lVert a_j\rVert , \] and the factor variance \(d_j^2\) is the variance arrow \(j\) carries. Because the arrows are perpendicular, the columns of \(\Gamma\) are perpendicular unit vectors, \(\Gamma'\Gamma=I\): \(\Gamma\) is a rotation (possibly with a reflection), which turns space without stretching or squishing anything. Reading \(\mathbf x_t=\Gamma D\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) from right to left, one transformation after the other (3Blue1Brown, chapter 4): \(D\) stretches the round cloud of shocks along the axes (a diagonal matrix just scales each basis vector), and \(\Gamma\) turns the stretched cloud into place. The covariance matrix is \(S=AA'=\Gamma D^2\Gamma'\). Undoing a product of transformations means undoing the last one first, so \[ A^{-1}=\big(\Gamma D\big)^{-1}=D^{-1}\,\Gamma' , \] where a rotation is undone by its transpose. Indeed, \(\Gamma'\Gamma=I\) says that applying \(\Gamma\) and then \(\Gamma'\) changes nothing, so \(\Gamma'\) is the inverse of \(\Gamma\), \(\Gamma^{-1}=\Gamma'\) (for a square matrix, a matrix that undoes it from one side also undoes it from the other, so \(\Gamma\Gamma'=I\) as well). The two layers come off one at a time: Undo the rotation. Turning the data back gives the factors, the principal component scores, \[ \mathbf f_t=\Gamma'\mathbf x_t,\qquad f_{tj}=\gamma_j'\mathbf x_t . \] Each score is an inner product with a unit vector, so it is the signed length of the projection of the week onto the direction of arrow \(j\) (3Blue1Brown, chapter 9). Put differently, \(\Gamma'\) is a change of basis (3Blue1Brown, chapter 13): \(\mathbf f_t\) describes the same week in coordinates whose axes are the arrows. The stretch is still in: the scores on component \(j\) have variance \(d_j^2\). Undo the stretch. Dividing each score by its standard deviation gives the shocks back, \[ \boldsymbol\varepsilon_t=D^{-1}\mathbf f_t,\qquad \varepsilon_{tj}=f_{tj}/d_j, \] the standardised scores, with variance one. The second figure runs the same week backwards, from the data to the shocks. This time the purple arrows follow the two variables: in the data panel they are the axes, one unit of Coca-Cola and one unit of Pepsi. Each arrow is where \(\Gamma'\) sends one unit of a variable, \(\Gamma'e_i\), which is row \(i\) of \(\Gamma\), so the arrows are the rows of \(\Gamma\). Because \(\Gamma\) is a rotation, the picture is the data panel turned, with nothing stretched: the inner product of a point with an arrow is that week’s value of the variable, \(x_{ti}=\gamma_{i1}f_{t1}+\gamma_{i2}f_{t2}\), and distances between points are distances between weeks. The right panel is the other common version, the standardised biplot. Undoing the stretch squishes the points into the round cloud of shocks, so for the inner product to still give the data, the stretch has to move onto the arrows: they are the rows of \(A=\Gamma D\), and \(x_{ti}=a_{i1}\varepsilon_{t1}+a_{i2}\varepsilon_{t2}\). Section 4.2.5 shows how to read biplots. 4.2.4 Dropping the short arrows Because the first arrow carries 95% of the variance, dropping the second loses little: \[ \mathbf x_t\approx \varepsilon_{t1}\,a_1=f_{t1}\,\gamma_1 . \] Each week is described by one number, its score \(f_{t1}\), its position along the market direction: the dimension reduction of the Introduction. The figure below turns the second arrow off. On the left, each week’s prediction \(\hat{\mathbf x}_t=f_{t1}\gamma_1\) is its projection onto the line of the first arrow, and the segment joining it to the actual week is the part that was dropped, \(\varepsilon_{t2}a_2\), perpendicular to the line. On the right, the predictions are plotted against the actual sales. Its value comes with more variables, where it shows the first two of many components: a map of the observations and the variables at once (the states in Section 4.5). Because \(x_{ti}=\gamma_{i1}f_{t1}+\gamma_{i2}f_{t2}\), it is read with three rules, exact when all components are shown and approximate when some are dropped: Point and arrow. A week far out in the direction of the Pepsi arrow sold a lot of Pepsi: its value on a variable is its projection onto that variable’s arrow, times the arrow’s length. Distances between points are the Euclidean distances between the observations (Chapter 2), because a rotation does not change distances. With more than two variables, the biplot shows only the first two components, and the distances on the map leave out the differences along the dropped ones: they are never longer than the true distances. Arrow lengths. With all components, every arrow has length one (the rows of a rotation). When the biplot keeps only the first two of \(p\) components, arrow \(i\) has length \(\sqrt{\gamma_{i1}^2+\gamma_{i2}^2}\le1\): the shorter it is, the more of variable \(i\) lies in the dropped components, and the less the map says about it. The two versions of the biplot in the backward figure come with two names for their arrows. In the scores version, the arrows are the rows of \(\Gamma\), and the entries of \(\Gamma\) are called the weights: they say how each score is computed, \(f_{tj}=\gamma_{1j}x_{t1}+\gamma_{2j}x_{t2}\). In the standardised version, the arrows are the rows of \(A=\Gamma D\), called the loadings: one standard deviation of component \(j\) moves variable \(i\) by \(a_{ij}=\gamma_{ij}d_j\), and divided by the standard deviation \(s_i\) of the variable this is the correlation between variable and component. Software uses the word “loadings” for both, so it pays to check which one is meant. Turn this around: project the data onto any direction, and ask which direction makes the projections spread out most. The answer is the first arrow again, now reached from the data alone. 4.3.1 A score along a direction Section 4.2 had two scores per week, one for each arrow: \(f_{t1}=\gamma_1'\mathbf x_t\) and \(f_{t2}=\gamma_2'\mathbf x_t\). Here we look at the first one only, a single linear combination of the two variables, and leave its direction open: \(\gamma_1=(\gamma_{11},\gamma_{21})'\) is any vector of length one, \(\gamma_1'\gamma_1=\gamma_{11}^2+\gamma_{21}^2=1\), not yet the PCA direction. Drop every week onto the line through the origin (the mean) in that direction. Its position on the line is its score, \[ f_{t1}=\gamma_1'\mathbf x_t=\gamma_{11}\,x_{t1}+\gamma_{21}\,x_{t2}, \] a weighted sum of the week’s deviations from the mean, exactly as in the scores of Section 4.2. The scores have mean zero, because the \(\mathbf x_t\) do. Their sample variance is therefore the sum of squared scores divided by \(n-1\), and writing the square as \(f_{t1}^2=(\gamma_1'\mathbf x_t)(\mathbf x_t'\gamma_1)\) lets \(\gamma_1\) move outside the sum: \[ s_{f_1}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t=1}^n f_{t1}^2 =\gamma_1'\Big(\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbf x_t\mathbf x_t'\Big)\gamma_1 =\gamma_1'S\,\gamma_1 , \] since the matrix in the middle is the sample covariance matrix of the centred data (Chapter 3). Written out, \(\gamma_1'S\gamma_1=\gamma_{11}^2s_1^2+2\gamma_{11}\gamma_{21}s_{12}+\gamma_{21}^2s_2^2\), the rule for the variance of a linear combination (Section 3.5.4). This is the same quantity as the squared length of the first arrow. With \(q=(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)'\), the first column of \(Q(\varphi)\), the first arrow is \(a_1=S^{1/2}q\), so \(\lVert a_1\rVert^2=q'S^{1/2}S^{1/2}q=q'Sq\): the variance of the scores along \(q\). The variance is largest at an angle of about 47 degrees, where it reaches 2.00, and smallest at the perpendicular direction, where it is only 0.10. 4.3.2 The principal components So the longest first arrow points in the direction with the largest score variance. In this language, the first principal component is the direction \(\gamma_1\) with the largest score variance, \[ \max_{\gamma_1}\;\gamma_1'S\gamma_1\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \gamma_1'\gamma_1=1 . \] The constraint matters: without it, doubling \(\gamma_1\) would quadruple the variance, and there would be no maximum. It is the normalisation of Section 4.1, columns of \(\Gamma\) of length one, seen from the data side. The second principal component \(\gamma_2\) maximises \(\gamma_2'S\gamma_2\) in the same way, among all unit vectors perpendicular to the first, \(\gamma_2'\gamma_1=0\); the third is perpendicular to both, and so on, up to \(p\) components. The scores on the \(j\)-th component, \(f_{tj}=\gamma_j'\mathbf x_t\), are the new variables. 4.3.3 The best-fitting line The first component has a second description. By Pythagoras, the squared distance of a point from the centre splits into the squared score along the line plus the squared distance to the line: \[ \lVert \mathbf x_t\rVert^2=f_t^2+\big(\text{perpendicular distance of } \mathbf x_t \text{ to the line}\big)^2 . \] The left side does not depend on the line. So the line that maximises the sum of squared scores is the line that minimises the sum of squared perpendicular distances: the first principal component is the line of best fit in the perpendicular sense. Regression fits a different line, because it minimises the vertical distances: it treats one variable as given and the other as the outcome, the assumption the Introduction questioned. With many variables there are too many angles to try. Linear algebra finds them directly, with an idea worth learning on its own: eigenvectors (3Blue1Brown, chapter 14). This section shows what they are and why the PCA directions are eigenvectors of \(S\). 4.4.1 Vectors that stay on their line A matrix moves the whole plane (the Introduction, and 3Blue1Brown, chapter 3). Take the covariance matrix \(S\) itself as such a movement: it sends each point \(v\) to \(Sv\). Most points are knocked off their own line, the line through the origin and \(v\) (its span). The points on a few special lines stay on them and are only stretched or squished: \[ Sv=\lambda v . \] Such a \(v\) is an eigenvector of \(S\), and the stretch factor \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue (3Blue1Brown, chapter 14). The slider applies the movement gradually, from nothing at all (the identity) to \(S\), for the Coke and Pepsi \(S\). The points on the blue line, at 46.5 degrees, stay on it and are stretched by \(\lambda_1=2.00\); those on the red line, at 136.5 degrees, stay on it and are squished by \(\lambda_2=0.10\). These are the two directions of the PCA arrows, and the stretch factors are the factor variances \(d_1^2\) and \(d_2^2\). The next subsection shows that this is no coincidence. 4.4.2 Why the PCA directions are eigenvectors Start from the covariance matrix and the PCA split of Section 4.2, \(A=\Gamma D\) with \(\Gamma\) a rotation and \(D\) diagonal: \[ S=AA'=(\Gamma D)(\Gamma D)'=\Gamma D D'\Gamma'=\Gamma D^2\Gamma' , \] using \((\Gamma D)'=D'\Gamma'\) and \(D'=D\) for a diagonal matrix. Now multiply both sides by \(\Gamma\) on the right. Because \(\Gamma'\Gamma=I\), the last two matrices cancel: \[ S\Gamma=\Gamma D^2\Gamma'\Gamma=\Gamma D^2 . \] Read this column by column. Column \(j\) of \(S\Gamma\) is \(S\gamma_j\). Column \(j\) of \(\Gamma D^2\) is \(d_j^2\gamma_j\), because multiplying by a diagonal matrix on the right just scales each column. So \[ S\gamma_j=d_j^2\,\gamma_j , \] which is exactly the eigenvector equation: each PCA direction \(\gamma_j\) is an eigenvector of \(S\), and its eigenvalue is \(d_j^2\), the variance of factor \(j\). In the figure, the points on the blue line are stretched by \(d_1^2\) and those on the red line by \(d_2^2\). And because PCA makes the first arrow as long as possible, the first component is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, the second the one with the next largest, and so on. The connection also runs the other way, and that is how PCA is computed in practice. A matrix whose eigenvectors span the space can be written as \[ S=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}, \] with the eigenvectors as the columns of \(Q\) and the eigenvalues in the diagonal matrix \(\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p)\), read from right to left: \(Q^{-1}\) changes to the coordinates of the eigenvectors, \(\Lambda\) stretches each axis, and \(Q\) changes back (3Blue1Brown, chapters 13 and 14). This is the eigendecomposition. For a general matrix, \(Q\) is not a rotation and \(Q^{-1}\) has to be computed. Covariance matrices are special: they are symmetric, \(S'=S\), and for a symmetric matrix the eigenvectors can always be chosen perpendicular and of length one (the spectral theorem). Then \(Q\) is a rotation, \(Q^{-1}=Q'\), and \[ S=Q\Lambda Q' \] has exactly the form of the PCA split \(S=\Gamma D^2\Gamma'\): \(\Gamma=Q\) and \(D^2=\Lambda\), up to the order and signs of the columns. The eigenvalues of a covariance matrix are variances, so they are never negative. One call to eigen() therefore replaces the slider: S <- cov(cola) e <- eigen(S) e$values # eigenvalues: the factor variances d_j^2 ## [1] 2.00131488 0.09868512 e$vectors # eigenvectors: the directions gamma_j (columns), up to sign ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.6882736 -0.7254512 ## [2,] 0.7254512 0.6882736 A <- e$vectors %*% diag(sqrt(e$values)) # the PCA choice of A = Gamma D A %*% t(A) # reproduces S ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 1.00 0.95 ## [2,] 0.95 1.10 The \(j\)-th principal component is the eigenvector \(\gamma_j\) of \(S\) with the \(j\)-th largest eigenvalue, and the variance of its scores is that eigenvalue, \(\lambda_j=d_j^2\). From here on the chapter writes \(\lambda_j\) for the variance of the \(j\)-th component. What Sections 4.1 and 4.2 showed about the factor variances now reads as a statement about eigenvalues: they add up to the total variance, \(\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_p=\operatorname{tr}(S)\), so component \(j\) carries the share \(\lambda_j/\operatorname{tr}(S)\) of it. For Coke and Pepsi the market component carries 95%. PCA of the covariance matrix finds the variable with the most units, not the most interesting direction. The right panel shows the remedy: standardise each variable first, \(z_{tj}=(x_{tj}-\bar x_j)/s_j\). Standardised values do not depend on the units, so neither do their components. The covariance matrix of standardised variables is the correlation matrix \(R\); for two variables its components are always the sum and the difference, \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)'\) and \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1)'\) (Section 4.4). PCA is not scale-invariant: changing the units of a variable changes the components, not just their units (Everitt and Hothorn, Section 3.4). When the variables are measured in different units, use PCA of the correlation matrix. Every variable then has variance one, \(\operatorname{tr}(R)=p\), and each starts with an equal claim on the components. Working with \(S\) is appropriate when all variables share a unit and their variances are comparable (sales of two brands in the same units, test scores on the same scale). 4.5.2 More variables: the states With more variables and very different units, the effect is extreme. Each arrow’s coordinates, read on the red axes at the top and right, are the variable’s weights on the two components. So: an arrow that points almost horizontally belongs mainly to the first component, one that points almost vertically to the second; two arrows pointing in opposite directions along one line form a contrast: a component that runs along that line separates states high on one variable from states high on the other. The illiteracy and life-expectancy arrows lie almost on the horizontal axis, pointing in opposite directions (weights -0.47 and 0.42 on the first component, 0.13 and -0.06 on the second). The first component (59% of the variance) is therefore mainly the contrast between illiteracy and life expectancy, with murder joining illiteracy on the left and graduation, frost and income joining life expectancy on the right: an index of general well-being. The southern states (Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, South Carolina) sit at the left, the northern plains (Minnesota, North Dakota, Iowa, Utah) at the right. The income arrow points mostly upwards (weight 0.72 on the second component, the largest of all), so the second component (16%) is mainly income. Murder and frost point in opposite directions along a diagonal: they contrast on both components, and on the second one murder goes up with income and frost goes down. States high on the second component are richer and warmer, with more murders (Alaska, California, Hawaii, Florida, Nevada at the top). The arrow lengths show how well the map represents each variable. With all six components every arrow would have length one. Here the income arrow is the longest (0.78): income lies mostly in the plane of the first two components, and the map shows it well. The life-expectancy arrow is the shortest (0.42), followed by illiteracy (0.49): much of their variation lies in the four dropped components, so the map says less about them, and states that look alike on the map can still differ in life expectancy. These labels are interpretations, not facts: they come from reading weights, and two components keep 76% of the variance, not all of it. Section 4.8 returns to this. The distances between the states on the map approximate their Euclidean distances in the six standardised variables. (The arrows are drawn four times longer than they are; the red axes give their scale.)
