All \(p\) components together reproduce the data exactly. The point of PCA is to keep fewer. There is no single correct number; Everitt and Hothorn (Section 3.8) list the common rules of thumb: Percentage of variance. Keep enough components to explain a chosen share of the total variance, usually between 70% and 90%. Above-average eigenvalues. Keep the components with \(\lambda_j\) above the average eigenvalue, \(\operatorname{tr}(S)/p\), the components that explain more than an average variable. For a correlation matrix the average is one: the Kaiser rule \(\lambda_j>1\). Jolliffe (1972) found in simulations that this drops too many components and suggested \(\lambda_j>0.7\) instead. Scree plot. Plot \(\lambda_j\) against \(j\) and look for an elbow, where the curve changes from steep to flat (Cattell 1966; scree is the rubble at the foot of a cliff). Keep the components before the flat part. A variant plots \(\log\lambda_j\). fig_scree <- function() { mk <- function(lam, name) tibble(data = name, j = seq_along(lam), lambda = lam, cum = cumsum(lam) / sum(lam)) d <- mk(st_lam, "US states (6 variables)") ggplot(d, aes(j, lambda)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = col_a2, linetype = 2) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.7, colour = col_a2, linetype = 3) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.6) + geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(100 * cum), "%")), nudge_y = 0.3, size = 3.3, colour = "grey30") + geom_text(data = tibble(y = c(1, 0.7), lab = c("1 (Kaiser)", "0.7 (Jolliffe)")), aes(x = 6, y = y, label = lab), hjust = 1, vjust = c(-0.4, 1.4), colour = col_a2, size = 3.3) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) + labs(x = "component", y = expression("eigenvalue"~lambda[j]~"(variance of the component)"), subtitle = "Labels: cumulative share of the total variance") } # draw the figure fig_scree() The rules disagree. For the states, 70% asks for 2 components and 90% for 4; the Kaiser rule keeps 1 (the second eigenvalue, 0.99, misses the cut-off by a hair), Jolliffe’s 0.7 keeps 3, and the elbow at component 2 says one. These are guides, not tests: choose with the purpose in mind. Two components are needed for a scatterplot; an index needs one; an input to a later analysis may need more. Check your understanding In a scree plot, the elbow marks the component with the largest eigenvalue where the eigenvalues stop falling steeply and level off the component that explains exactly 50% where the eigenvalues become negative For a correlation matrix, the Kaiser rule keeps components with eigenvalue above 1 because 1 is the variance of each standardised variable, so such components explain more than one variable eigenvalues above 1 are statistically significant the total variance is 1 components with \(\lambda<1\) are negatively correlated Answers 1 b. 2 a. 4.7 Reconstruction and unusual observations With \(p\) variables, keeping only a few components loses information. How much, and for which observations? Because \(\Gamma\) is a rotation, the scores can be turned back into the data: \(\mathbf x_t=\Gamma \mathbf f_t =\sum_{j=1}^p f_{tj}\gamma_j\). Keeping only the first \(m\) terms gives the best approximation from \(m\) numbers, \[ \hat{\mathbf x}_t=\sum_{j=1}^m f_{tj}\gamma_j , \] and the sum of the squared errors over all observations and variables is \((n-1)(\lambda_{m+1}+\dots+\lambda_p)\): the variance of the dropped components. The covariance matrix is approximated in the same way, \(S\approx A_mA_m'\) with the first \(m\) columns of \(A\) (Everitt and Hothorn, Section 3.7). fig_reconstruct <- function(states = c("Alaska", "Hawaii", "Texas")) { Z <- scale(X6); G <- st_cor$rotation; Y <- st_cor$x rec <- function(s, m) drop(G[, 1:m, drop = FALSE] %*% Y[s, 1:m]) # x-hat = sum of the first m score * weight d <- purrr::map_dfr(states, function(s) bind_rows( tibble(state = s, var = colnames(X6), m = "actual", z = Z[s, ]), purrr::map_dfr(1:3, function(k) tibble(state = s, var = colnames(X6), z = rec(s, k), m = paste0("m = ", k))))) |> mutate(var = factor(var, levels = colnames(X6)), state = factor(state, levels = states)) ggplot(d, aes(var, z)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_col(data = filter(d, m == "actual"), fill = "grey80", width = 0.7) + geom_point(data = filter(d, m != "actual"), aes(colour = m, shape = m), size = 2.6, position = position_dodge(width = 0.55)) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("m = 1" = col_a1, "m = 2" = "#7b4fb5", "m = 3" = col_a2), name = "reconstruction") + scale_shape_manual(values = c("m = 1" = 16, "m = 2" = 17, "m = 3" = 15), name = "reconstruction") + facet_wrap(~ state, ncol = 3) + labs(x = NULL, y = "standardised value (bars: actual)") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1), legend.position = "top") } # draw the figure fig_reconstruct() Texas follows the common pattern: one component (blue) already gets the signs and rough sizes of all six standardised values. Alaska and Hawaii do not: one component misses them badly, and only two or three components come close. Recall from Section 2.6 that these are the states with unusual combinations. This is no coincidence: the squared Mahalanobis distance is the sum of the standardised squared scores, \[ d_t^2=\mathbf x_t'S^{-1}\mathbf x_t=\sum_{j=1}^p\frac{f_{tj}^2}{\lambda_j}=\sum_{j=1}^p\varepsilon_{tj}^2, \] because \(S^{-1}=\Gamma D^{-2}\Gamma'\). A large score on a small component, a direction in which the cloud is thin, counts heavily. Unusual states are exactly those that the first components describe badly. Z <- scale(X) for (m in 1:4) { Zhat <- pc$x[, 1:m, drop = FALSE] %*% t(pc$rotation[, 1:m, drop = FALSE]) # reconstruction from m scores cat(m, "components: squared error", round(sum((Z - Zhat)^2), 1), "= (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues", round(49 * sum(pc$sdev[-(1:m)]^2), 1), "\n") } ## 1 components: squared error 119.8 = (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues 119.8 ## 2 components: squared error 71.4 = (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues 71.4 ## 3 components: squared error 32.7 = (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues 32.7 ## 4 components: squared error 17 = (n - 1) x dropped eigenvalues 17 Check your understanding Reconstructing standardised data from the first \(m\) components leaves a squared error equal to zero \((n-1)\) times the sum of the dropped eigenvalues \((n-1)\) times the sum of the kept eigenvalues the largest eigenvalue A state with a large score on the last component is typical is unusual in a direction where the cloud is thin, so it has a large Mahalanobis distance has a large value on every variable has been reconstructed exactly by the first component Answers 1 b. 2 b. 4.8 What PCA is, and what it is not 4.8.1 One choice of structural form PCA is one answer to the identification problem of the Introduction: of all the matrices \(A\) with \(AA'=S\), it picks the one whose first column is longest. That is a choice made for convenience (order the directions by variance), not one forced by the data. For the flights, where we know the true shocks from the manual, the first principal component explains 91% of the variance, but it is neither the headwind nor the load: it is a mixture of both. cloud_pts <- function(X, alpha = 0.45) geom_point(data = tibble(x = X[, 1], y = X[, 2]), aes(x, y), colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = alpha, size = 1.5) fig_pca_vs_truth <- function() { S <- cov(air_X); e <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE) G <- e$vectors; if (G[1, 1] < 0) G[, 1] <- -G[, 1]; if (det(G) < 0) G[, 2] <- -G[, 2] A_pca <- G %*% diag(sqrt(e$values)) el <- ellipse_xy(sym_root(S), 1); el <- tibble(x = el[1, ], y = el[2, ]) panel <- function(M, labs, title) { lab <- tibble(x = M[1, ] * (1 + 0.9 / sqrt(colSums(M^2))), y = M[2, ] * (1 + 0.9 / sqrt(colSums(M^2))), txt = labs, col = c(col_a1, col_a2)) ggplot() + axes0 + cloud_pts(air_X, 0.25) + geom_path(data = el, aes(x, y), linewidth = 0.9) + geom_segment(data = tibble(xend = M[1, ], yend = M[2, ], col = c(col_a1, col_a2)), aes(0, 0, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = I(col)), linewidth = 1.5, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed")) + geom_label(data = lab, aes(x, y, label = txt, colour = I(col)), size = 4, fontface = "bold", label.size = 0, fill = alpha("white", 0.8), lineheight = 0.9) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.2, 4.2), ylim = c(-4.2, 4.2)) + labs(title = title, x = "flight time (min)", y = "fuel (100 kg)") } panel(A_pca, c("PC1", "PC2"), "PCA: longest first column") + panel(air_A, c("headwind", "load"), "The true shocks (from the manual)") } # draw the figure fig_pca_vs_truth() So it is tempting, but risky, to give components names such as “all-round ability” or “quality of life”. Everitt and Hothorn quote Marriott (1974): “no mathematical method is, or could be, designed to give physically meaningful results.” A component that has an obvious meaning reflects a strongly structured data set, or luck. PCA is safest as a tool for description and compression: a low-dimensional map of the data, an index, or fewer inputs for a later analysis. 4.8.2 Practical points Correlation is needed. PCA can only compress correlated variables. If the variables are uncorrelated and standardised, every eigenvalue is one and no component is better than any other. Scale. Results depend on the units unless the variables are standardised (Section 4.5). Outliers. One observation can change the correlations, and hence the components (the PNG athlete). Look at the data first, as in Chapter 2. Signs and order. Signs are arbitrary. Components with nearly equal eigenvalues are unstable: a slightly different sample can swap them or mix them. Sample size. Larger samples give more stable components, especially when eigenvalues are close together. Rules such as \(n>100\) or \(n>5p\) have little evidence behind them (Everitt and Hothorn, Section 3.12). Regression on components. Highly correlated explanatory variables can be replaced by their first few components (principal components regression). The components with the largest variance need not be the ones that best predict the outcome, however: Everitt and Hothorn’s air-pollution example finds low-variance components that matter (Section 3.10.3). Check your understanding For the flights, the first principal component is exactly the headwind shock is exactly the load shock is a mixture of both: PCA picks a convenient rotation, not the true one does not exist because the shocks are independent Six uncorrelated standardised variables give a correlation-matrix PCA in which the first component explains everything every eigenvalue is 1, so there is nothing to compress the components are the variables in order of their means the scree plot has a sharp elbow Answers 1 c. 2 b. 4.9 Two sets of variables: canonical correlation PCA looks at the relations within one set of variables. Sometimes the question is about the relation between two sets: aptitude tests and achievement tests, plant growth and weather, or, for the states, education (illiteracy, high-school graduation) and health and safety (life expectancy, murder). Many pairwise correlations between the sets are hard to summarise, and the correlations within each set get in the way. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA, Everitt and Hothorn, Section 3.13) replaces each set by a few linear combinations. With the first set \(x\) (\(q_1\) variables) and the second set \(y\) (\(q_2\) variables), find weights \(a_1\) and \(b_1\) such that the two canonical variates \(u_1=a_1'x\) and \(v_1=b_1'y\) have the largest possible correlation \(R_1\), the first canonical correlation. Then find a second pair \((u_2,v_2)\) with the largest correlation \(R_2\) among combinations uncorrelated with the first pair, and so on, up to \(s=\min(q_1,q_2)\) pairs. Like the principal components, the weights are eigenvectors: with \(R_{11}\) and \(R_{22}\) the correlation matrices within the two sets and \(R_{12}=R_{21}'\) the correlations between them, the \(a_i\) are the eigenvectors of \(E_1=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}R_{22}^{-1}R_{21}\), the \(b_i\) those of \(E_2=R_{22}^{-1}R_{21}R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}\), and the eigenvalues are the squared canonical correlations \(R_i^2\). For the states, the first canonical correlation is 0.71. In standardised variables, the first pair is approximately \[ u_1\propto-0.98\,\text{Illiteracy}+0.19\,\text{HSGrad},\qquad v_1\propto0.30\,\text{LifeExp}-0.95\,\text{Murder}: \] low illiteracy goes with low murder rates. The second canonical correlation, 0.37, is much weaker. Its pair puts positive weight on both variables of each set, \[ u_2\propto0.60\,\text{Illiteracy}+0.80\,\text{HSGrad},\qquad v_2\propto0.75\,\text{LifeExp}+0.66\,\text{Murder}: \] what is left once the first pair is accounted for: a weak tendency for states with both more illiteracy and more high-school graduates to have both longer lives and more murders. With two variables per set, \(u_2\) is the only education index left that is uncorrelated with \(u_1\), so it plays the role of a residual: a second education index, not a regression residual, but the direction in the education variables that \(u_1\) leaves out. The same holds for \(v_2\) and health and safety. fig_cca <- function() { U <- Zst[, c("Illiteracy", "HSGrad")] %*% cc_states$xcoef V <- Zst[, c("LifeExp", "Murder")] %*% cc_states$ycoef U <- U * sqrt(nrow(U) - 1); V <- V * sqrt(nrow(V) - 1) # canonical variates with variance 1 s1 <- sign(cc_states$xcoef["HSGrad", 1]) # first pair: high = more educated s2 <- sign(cc_states$xcoef["HSGrad", 2]) # second pair: positive weights d <- tibble(abb = state.abb, u1 = s1 * U[, 1], v1 = s1 * V[, 1], u2 = s2 * U[, 2], v2 = s2 * V[, 2]) p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(u1, v1)) + geom_point(colour = col_a1, size = 2) + geom_text_repel(aes(label = abb), size = 2.8, colour = "grey35", seed = 5, max.overlaps = 15) + labs(title = sprintf("First pair: correlation %.2f", cc_states$cor[1]), x = expression(italic(u)[1]*": education"), y = expression(italic(v)[1]*": health and safety")) p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(u2, v2)) + geom_point(colour = col_a2, size = 2) + geom_text_repel(aes(label = abb), size = 2.8, colour = "grey35", seed = 5, max.overlaps = 15) + labs(title = sprintf("Second pair: correlation %.2f", cc_states$cor[2]), x = expression(italic(u)[2]*": education, second index"), y = expression(italic(v)[2]*": health and safety, second index")) p1 + p2 } # draw the figure fig_cca() Most states lie close to the line in the left panel. Nevada stands out at the bottom right: well educated, but with a high murder rate. Zs <- scale(X) cc <- cancor(Zs[, c("Illiteracy", "HS Grad")], Zs[, c("Life Exp", "Murder")]) cc$cor # canonical correlations ## [1] 0.7102436 0.3651655 R <- cor(X[, c("Illiteracy", "HS Grad", "Life Exp", "Murder")]) E1 <- solve(R[1:2, 1:2]) %*% R[1:2, 3:4] %*% solve(R[3:4, 3:4]) %*% R[3:4, 1:2] sqrt(eigen(E1)$values) # the same, from the eigenvalues of E1 ## [1] 0.7102436 0.3651655 CCA is used less than the other methods in this course because its variates are often hard to interpret (Everitt and Hothorn’s examples, head sizes of brothers and depression in Los Angeles, show both a clear and a less clear case). It is the natural generalisation of the multiple correlation of regression to several outcomes. The split needs a normalisation: ones on the diagonal (Cholesky, the regressor and the residual; symmetric root, each roommate’s own GPA), outside facts (structural), or columns of length one (PCA, so that the factor variances add up to the total variance). Every \(A\) with \(AA'=S\) fits the data; the squared length of each arrow (column) is the variance its shock carries. PCA turns the arrows until the first one is longest, then the second, and so on; the arrows come out perpendicular, so \(A=\Gamma D\) is a stretch followed by a rotation. The scores \(\mathbf f_t=\Gamma'\mathbf x_t\) undo the rotation, the standardised scores undo the stretch too. Equivalently, the first principal component is the unit vector \(\gamma_1\) whose scores \(\gamma_1'\mathbf x_t\) have the largest variance; it is also the line closest to the cloud in the perpendicular sense. The components are the eigenvectors of \(S\), the directions that \(S\) only stretches, and their variances the eigenvalues. In the eigenbasis the covariance matrix is diagonal, \(Q'SQ=\Lambda\), and \(S=Q\Lambda Q'\) is the PCA split with \(\Gamma=Q\), \(D^2=\Lambda\): the scores are uncorrelated, and the eigenvalues add up to the total variance. PCA depends on the units: rescaling one variable swings the components towards it. With different units, use the correlation matrix (standardised variables). How many components is a judgement: share of variance, eigenvalues above average (Kaiser, Jolliffe), the scree plot. The biplot draws \(\mathbf x_t=\Gamma\mathbf f_t\): scores as points, rows of \(\Gamma\) (the weights) as arrows; with standardised scores, the arrows are the rows of \(A=\Gamma D\) (the loadings). Short arrows mark variables that the first two components represent poorly. The first \(m\) components give the best \(m\)-dimensional reconstruction; observations that it misses are the unusual combinations of Chapter 2. PCA is a convenient rotation, not a discovery of the true forces: use it to describe and compress, and label components with care. Canonical correlation extends the idea to two sets of variables. PCA keeps the directions in which the data vary most, and drops the rest. 4.10.1 Further reading Everitt and Hothorn (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Chapter 3 (principal components analysis, Sections 3.1 to 3.12; canonical correlation analysis, Section 3.13). 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra, chapters 9 (dot products and projections), 13 (change of basis) and 14 (eigenvectors and eigenvalues).
